1.lecture:
§1 · Links, joints, and the chain they make

Machinery is not made of forces first. It is made of rigid bodies connected so that only certain motions survive, and the forces follow from the motion that is left. A link is one of those rigid bodies; a joint, or kinematic pair, is a connection that removes some of the freedom between two links. Connect links in a closed loop and you have a kinematic chain; fix one link to the earth and the chain becomes a mechanism.

A free rigid body in a plane has three degrees of freedom — two translations and a rotation. Joints are graded by how much of that they take away. A pin (revolute) and a slider (prismatic) each leave exactly one relative freedom, so each removes two; they are called lower pairs because they touch over a surface. A cam pressed against a follower or a gear tooth pressed against another touches along a line, leaves two freedoms — rolling and sliding along the contact — and so removes only one. Those are higher pairs. The distinction is not cosmetic: it is the whole difference between the two terms in the count that follows.

§2 · Mobility, counted before anything is drawn

Add up what the links bring and subtract what the joints take. With \( N \) links one is grounded, so \( 3(N-1) \) freedoms enter; each lower pair removes two and each higher pair removes one.

Key relation — Kutzbach mobility criterion

\[ M = 3(N-1) - 2j_1 - j_2 \]

\( N \) counts links including the fixed one, \( j_1 \) counts lower pairs (pins and sliders) and \( j_2 \) counts higher pairs (cam and gear contacts). \( M \) is the number of inputs the mechanism needs before its geometry is fully determined.

For the four-bar in the figure, \( N=4 \) and \( j_1=4 \), so \( M = 3(3) - 8 = 1 \). One motor, one position — which is why the four-bar is everywhere. A slider-crank counts identically: four links again, three pins and one slider, \( M=1 \). A cam driving a translating follower has three links, two lower pairs and one higher pair: \( M = 3(2) - 4 - 1 = 1 \).

Read the other answers as verdicts, not failures. \( M = 0 \) is a structure — it does not move, which is exactly what a bracket should do. \( M < 0 \) is a statically indeterminate structure, over-constrained. \( M = 2 \) needs two inputs, like a robot arm with two motors. The count costs nothing and is done before geometry, which makes it the cheapest design check in the subject.

It has one honest limitation. Kutzbach counts joints, not where they are, so a chain with special proportions can move when the count says it cannot. A parallelogram linkage with a redundant fifth link duplicating an existing one counts as \( M = 0 \) yet runs perfectly, because the extra link is exactly parallel to the one it shadows — locomotive coupling rods work this way. A count of zero on a mechanism that visibly moves means the geometry is special, and special geometry is fragile: build that same linkage with real tolerances and it binds.

§3 · Grashof: which link is allowed a full turn

Mobility says a four-bar needs one input. It does not say that input can be a motor. For a link to be driven by a continuously rotating shaft it must be able to pass through every angle, and a four-bar only permits that for certain proportions.

Key relation — Grashof condition

\[ s + \ell \le p + q \]

\( s \) is the shortest link, \( \ell \) the longest, and \( p,q \) the other two. If the inequality holds, the shortest link can rotate fully relative to all the others; if it fails, no link can, and every link merely rocks.

Satisfying Grashof tells you a full rotation exists somewhere in the chain. Which motion you get depends on where the shortest link sits. Ground the link adjacent to the shortest and you get a crank-rocker: the short link spins, the far link oscillates — the wiper linkage, the oscillating conveyor, the classic rotation-to-oscillation converter. Ground the shortest link itself and both side links rotate fully: a double-crank, or drag-link, used where two shafts must both turn but at a deliberately uneven rate. Ground the link opposite the shortest and both side links rock while the coupler makes the full turn: a double-rocker. Fail the inequality and every inversion is a triple-rocker — useful for guided motion, useless for a motor.

The figure's linkage gives \( 40+120 = 160 \le 100+90 = 190 \). It is Grashof, the shortest link is the crank, and the crank is adjacent to ground, so it is a crank-rocker and a motor can drive it.

§4 · Inversions, and the angle that decides whether it is any good

Fixing a different link of the same chain produces an inversion. The relative motion between links is untouched — only the observer's anchor moves — yet the machine that results can be unrecognisable. The slider-crank makes the point better than any other chain. Ground the block and you have a reciprocating engine or compressor. Ground the crank and the cylinder swings: the oscillating-cylinder engine, and the Whitworth quick-return that gives a shaper its fast idle stroke. Ground the connecting rod and you get the hand pump. Four machines, one chain, one set of relative motions.

What separates a working linkage from a nominally correct one is the transmission angle \( \mu \), the angle between the coupler and the driven link. The force in the coupler is a push along its own line; only the component perpendicular to the driven link produces torque, and that component goes as \( \sin\mu \). At \( \mu = 90^\circ \) the transfer is perfect. As \( \mu \) approaches \( 0^\circ \) or \( 180^\circ \) the coupler force turns into bearing load and heat, the mechanism becomes sensitive to friction, and it can stall. Practice keeps \( \mu \ge 40^\circ \) through the whole cycle.

Apply it to the figure. At \( \theta_2 = 60^\circ \), \( \mu = 46.4^\circ \) — acceptable. But \( \mu \) is worst when the crank points straight at the far pivot, and there \( \mu = 29.0^\circ \). This linkage is Grashof, has \( M=1 \), and is still a poor design: once per revolution it works through an angle no designer would sign off. Shortening the crank from 40 to 25 mm lifts the worst case to 38.6°. Mobility and Grashof are gates; the transmission angle is the grade.

quiz.q:
Mobility of four chains

Problem. Count the mobility of each planar chain and say what it is. (a) A four-bar: 4 links, 4 pins. (b) A cam driving a translating roller follower: 3 links, 2 lower pairs, 1 higher pair. (c) A Watt six-bar: 6 links, 7 pins. (d) A proposed bracing linkage: 5 links, 6 pins.
quiz.solution:
Solution. Use \( M = 3(N-1) - 2j_1 - j_2 \) throughout.

(a) \( M = 3(4-1) - 2(4) - 0 = 9 - 8 = 1 \). One input, one configuration — a mechanism.

(b) \( M = 3(3-1) - 2(2) - 1 = 6 - 4 - 1 = 1 \). The higher pair removes only one freedom, which is exactly what leaves the follower free to be positioned by the cam.

(c) \( M = 3(6-1) - 2(7) = 15 - 14 = 1 \). Six-bars are built to keep \( M=1 \) while giving the designer more coupler curves than a four-bar can.

(d) \( M = 3(5-1) - 2(6) = 12 - 12 = 0 \). Not a mechanism — a structure.

Answer: (a) 1, (b) 1, (c) 1, (d) 0. Sanity check: only (d) differs, and it should — it was proposed as bracing. Had the answer come out \( -1 \) the bracing would still stand, but it would be over-constrained and would fight thermal expansion. Note also that (b) would have counted 0 if the cam contact had been treated as a lower pair; the one-freedom difference between line contact and surface contact is the entire result.

quiz.q:
Grashof classification in US customary units

Problem. Three four-bars are specified as (ground, crank, coupler, rocker) in inches: (a) (8, 2, 7, 5); (b) (3, 8, 7, 6); (c) (7, 6, 2.5, 8). For each, test the Grashof condition and name the mechanism obtained with the stated link grounded.
quiz.solution:
Solution. The condition \( s+\ell \le p+q \) is a comparison of lengths, so it is dimensionless and inches serve as well as millimetres — no conversion is needed.

(a) Sorted: 2, 5, 7, 8. \( s+\ell = 2+8 = 10 \le 5+7 = 12 \) ✓. The shortest link (2 in) is the crank, which is adjacent to the fixed ground link → crank-rocker.

(b) Sorted: 3, 6, 7, 8. \( s+\ell = 3+8 = 11 \le 6+7 = 13 \) ✓. The shortest link (3 in) is the ground itself → double-crank (drag-link): both side links turn fully.

(c) Sorted: 2.5, 6, 7, 8. \( s+\ell = 2.5+8 = 10.5 \le 6+7 = 13 \) ✓. The shortest link (2.5 in) is the coupler → double-rocker: both side links rock and the coupler makes the full revolution.

Answer: all three are Grashof; (a) crank-rocker, (b) drag-link, (c) double-rocker. Sanity check: the three cases share one chain type and differ only in which link is grounded — they are inversions, and they demonstrate that passing Grashof tells you a full rotation exists but not who performs it. A fourth set, (10, 4, 6, 5), gives \( 4+10 = 14 > 6+5 = 11 \): non-Grashof, so every inversion is a triple-rocker and none of them may be motor-driven.

quiz.q:
Transmission angle over a full revolution

Problem. For the linkage in the figure — ground 100 mm, crank 40 mm, coupler 120 mm, rocker 90 mm — find the transmission angle at \( \theta_2 = 60^\circ \), then at the two crank positions that give its extremes, and judge the design. Use \( \cos\mu = (r_3^2+r_4^2-d^2)/(2r_3r_4) \), where \( d \) is the distance from the moving crank pin A to the fixed pivot \( O_4 \).
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) At \( \theta_2 = 60^\circ \), A sits at \( (40\cos 60^\circ,\ 40\sin 60^\circ) = (20.00,\ 34.64) \) mm, so \( d = \sqrt{(100-20)^2 + 34.64^2} = \sqrt{6400+1200} = 87.18\ \mathrm{mm} \).

(2) \( \cos\mu = \frac{120^2+90^2-87.18^2}{2(120)(90)} = \frac{14400+8100-7600}{21600} = 0.6898 \), so \( \mu = 46.4^\circ \).

(3) \( \mu \) is monotonic in \( d \), and \( d \) is extreme when the crank lies along the ground line. At \( \theta_2 = 0^\circ \), \( d = 100-40 = 60\ \mathrm{mm} \): \( \cos\mu = (14400+8100-3600)/21600 = 0.8750 \Rightarrow \mu = 29.0^\circ \).

(4) At \( \theta_2 = 180^\circ \), \( d = 100+40 = 140\ \mathrm{mm} \): \( \cos\mu = (14400+8100-19600)/21600 = 0.1343 \Rightarrow \mu = 82.3^\circ \).

Answer: \( \mu = 46.4^\circ \) at 60°, ranging from 29.0° to 82.3° over the revolution. The minimum is well below the 40° guideline, so the design is rejected. Sanity check: the fix follows from the same arithmetic — the extremes come from \( d = r_1 \mp r_2 \), so shrinking the crank narrows the swing of \( d \). Recomputing with a 25 mm crank gives \( d = 75 \) to 125 mm and \( \mu_{\min} = 38.6^\circ \), nearly acceptable, at the cost of the rocker stroke the crank was sized to produce. That trade — stroke against transmission angle — is the whole of four-bar design.

quiz.q: A free rigid body in plane motion has how many degrees of freedom?
quiz.solution: Two translations and one rotation. That is why the mobility count opens with \( 3(N-1) \): every link but the grounded one brings three freedoms into the chain before any joint takes them away. Six is the answer in three dimensions, and using it by mistake in a planar count is the most common way to get a nonsense mobility.

quiz.q: A cam pressed against a follower is a higher pair because the contact
choices: is along a line, leaving two relative freedoms
quiz.solution: Higher and lower refer to the geometry of contact, not the load. A cam and its follower touch along a line and can both roll and slide there, so two relative freedoms survive and only one is removed — the \( j_2 \) term. A pin or slider touches over a surface, leaves one freedom, and removes two. Grading the pair wrongly changes the mobility by exactly one, which is usually the difference between a mechanism and a structure.

quiz.q: A planar chain is counted and gives \( M = 0 \). It is
quiz.solution: Zero mobility means no motion is available: the chain is a structure, and if it was meant to be a bracket that is the right answer. Over-constraint shows up as \( M < 0 \), where the chain would still not move but would also fight its own tolerances and thermal growth. The one caution is that Kutzbach counts joints and not their positions, so a chain with special proportions — parallel links, or a redundant link shadowing another — can move despite counting zero.

quiz.q: A four-bar has links 30, 90, 70 and 60 mm. Is it Grashof?
choices: Cannot be decided without knowing which link is grounded
quiz.solution: Sort the lengths: \( s=30 \), \( \ell=90 \), and the intermediates are 60 and 70. \( s+\ell = 120 \le 60+70 = 130 \), so the condition holds. Grounding does not enter the test at all — it decides which inversion you get (crank-rocker, drag-link or double-rocker) once the test has already been passed.

quiz.q: Grounding the shortest link of a Grashof four-bar produces a
quiz.solution: With the shortest link fixed, both links attached to it can complete full revolutions, giving the drag-link used where two shafts must both turn but at a deliberately uneven rate through the cycle. Grounding a link adjacent to the shortest gives the crank-rocker; grounding the link opposite gives the double-rocker, where the coupler makes the full turn. A triple-rocker is what every inversion becomes when the Grashof test fails.

quiz.q: Two mechanisms are inversions of the same kinematic chain. What is identical between them?
choices: The absolute path of every point
quiz.solution: An inversion changes which link is held to the earth, so the relative motion between any two links is untouched — that is the definition. Everything measured against ground does change: absolute paths, velocities and inertia forces are all different, which is why a slider-crank becomes an engine, a quick-return shaper or a hand pump depending on what is bolted down.

quiz.q: The force a coupler delivers to the driven link goes as
quiz.solution: The coupler is a two-force member, so it pushes along its own line. Resolve that push at the driven link: the component perpendicular to the link, which is the only one that makes torque, is proportional to \( \sin\mu \). At \( \mu = 90^\circ \) all of it is useful; at \( \mu = 30^\circ \) half of it is, and the rest becomes bearing load. That is why practice sets a floor of about 40° on the worst \( \mu \) in the cycle.

quiz.q: A four-bar passes Grashof and has \( M = 1 \), but its transmission angle falls to 22° once per revolution. The correct verdict is
choices: Poor: near that position the coupler force mostly becomes bearing load and the mechanism can stall
Poor, because a low transmission angle means the links are too long
Acceptable if the motor torque is doubled
quiz.solution: Mobility and Grashof are gates, not grades: they say a full rotation exists and one input controls it, and say nothing about how well force is passed. At 22° only \( \sin 22^\circ = 0.37 \) of the coupler force does useful work while the rest loads the bearings, so friction and load variation can stall the mechanism there. Doubling the motor torque drives the joint loads up with it rather than fixing the geometry; the real fix is to change the proportions, usually by shortening the crank relative to the ground link.

1.kuwait:
Applied case — the bracket that was moved 40 mm. An oscillating screen drive used a crank-rocker: ground 100 mm between the two fixed pivots, 40 mm crank, 120 mm coupler, 90 mm rocker — \( 40+120 = 160 \le 100+90 = 190 \), Grashof, motor-driven for years. During a plant modification a new pipe run fouled the motor pedestal, and the pedestal was moved 40 mm toward the rocker pivot. Nothing else was touched: same motor, same crank, same coupler, same rocker, same fasteners. The drive then stalled on start-up in some positions and ran in others, and the motor tripped on overload.

The ground link is a link. Shortening it from 100 to 60 mm changed the set to (60, 40, 120, 90): the shortest is still 40 and the longest still 120, but the other two now sum to \( 60+90 = 150 \), and \( 160 > 150 \). The linkage had become non-Grashof, and a non-Grashof four-bar has no fully rotating link at all. Checking the geometry angle by angle confirms it: the chain assembles at 307 of 360 crank angles and cannot be assembled at all within \( 26.4^\circ \) either side of the crank pointing at the far pivot. The motor was being asked to drive the crank into a position the linkage geometrically cannot occupy, so whether it started depended on where it had stopped.

Two practices follow. A pivot location is a design dimension with a tolerance, not a mounting convenience — the ground link deserves the same drawing control as the parts that visibly move. And any change to a linkage, including one that moves no moving part, is re-tested through Grashof and through the worst transmission angle before it is fitted; both tests are arithmetic on four numbers and take a minute.
1.recap:
• A link is a rigid body, a joint removes relative freedom, and a chain with one link fixed to earth is a mechanism.
  • Lower pairs (pins, sliders) contact over a surface and remove two freedoms; higher pairs (cam, gear tooth) contact along a line and remove one.
  • Kutzbach: \( M = 3(N-1) - 2j_1 - j_2 \). \( M=1 \) is a one-input mechanism, \( M=0 \) a structure, \( M<0 \) over-constrained.
  • The count ignores where the joints are, so special geometry — parallel or redundant links — can move while counting zero, and does so only while the tolerances hold.
  • Grashof, \( s+\ell \le p+q \), decides whether any link can be driven by a continuously rotating motor.
  • Which inversion you get depends on what is grounded: adjacent to the shortest gives a crank-rocker, the shortest itself gives a drag-link, opposite gives a double-rocker.
  • Inversions preserve relative motion between links and change everything measured against ground — one slider-crank chain gives an engine, a quick-return and a hand pump.
  • The transmission angle \( \mu \) grades a linkage: useful force goes as \( \sin\mu \), and \( \mu \) should stay above about 40° through the whole cycle.
  • The worked linkage is Grashof with \( M=1 \) and still poor: \( \mu \) falls to 29.0° once per revolution, fixed by shortening the crank at the cost of stroke.

2.lecture:
§1 · Closing the loop

A mechanism with \( M=1 \) has one input, so every other position must follow from it. The machinery for extracting them is one equation: go round the closed chain and arrive back where you started. Treat each link as a vector and the four-bar becomes

Key relation — vector loop closure

\[ r_2e^{i\theta_2} + r_3e^{i\theta_3} - r_4e^{i\theta_4} - r_1 = 0 \]

Real and imaginary parts give two scalar equations. With \( r_1 \ldots r_4 \) and the input \( \theta_2 \) known, they determine \( \theta_3 \) and \( \theta_4 \).

Two solutions satisfy those equations — the open and crossed circuits, mirror images across the line from the crank pin to the far pivot. A physical linkage is assembled into one of them and stays there; it cannot jump circuits without being taken apart. Choosing the wrong root is the standard way a mechanism analysis produces a mechanism nobody built.

Solving by hand is easier as geometry than as algebra. Locate the crank pin A from \( \theta_2 \), measure the distance \( d \) from A to the fixed pivot \( O_4 \), and then A, \( O_4 \) and the coupler pin B form a triangle whose three sides are all known: \( d \), \( r_3 \) and \( r_4 \). Two applications of the cosine rule finish it. At \( \theta_2 = 60^\circ \) on the linkage in the figure, A is at (20.00, 34.64) mm, \( d = 87.18 \) mm, and the triangle gives \( \theta_3 = 24.95^\circ \) and \( \theta_4 = 71.34^\circ \). If \( d \) ever falls outside \( |r_3-r_4| \) to \( r_3+r_4 \), no triangle exists and the linkage cannot be assembled at that crank angle — which is the Grashof condition of Lesson 1 arriving again, this time as a broken square root.

§2 · Velocity, by differentiating the loop

Differentiate the closure equation once with respect to time. The link lengths are constant, so only the angles move, and the result is linear in the unknown angular velocities — which is why velocity analysis is always easier than position analysis.

Key relation — four-bar angular velocities

\[ \omega_3=\frac{r_2\omega_2\sin(\theta_4-\theta_2)}{r_3\sin(\theta_3-\theta_4)}, \qquad \omega_4=\frac{r_2\omega_2\sin(\theta_2-\theta_3)}{r_4\sin(\theta_4-\theta_3)} \]

Both are proportional to \( \omega_2 \): double the input speed and every velocity in the mechanism doubles, while the geometry is untouched.

With \( \omega_2 = 10 \) rad/s the linkage gives \( \omega_3 = -0.905 \) rad/s and \( \omega_4 = 3.525 \) rad/s. The sign on \( \omega_3 \) is information, not an error: the coupler is rotating the opposite way to the crank at this instant. The rocker turns at 0.3525 of the crank speed — at this instant only.

§3 · Instant centres, and the audit they provide

Any two rigid bodies in plane motion have, at each instant, one point where their velocities are equal: the instant centre. If one body is the ground, the instant centre is the point of the moving body that is momentarily at rest, and the body is turning about it as if pinned there. A mechanism of \( N \) links has \( N(N-1)/2 \) of them — six for a four-bar.

Four are free: the four pin joints are instant centres by inspection (\( I_{12}, I_{23}, I_{34}, I_{14} \)). The remaining two come from the Aronhold-Kennedy theorem: the three instant centres shared by any three bodies lie on one straight line. Apply it to links 1, 2 and 4 and \( I_{24} \) must lie on the line \( I_{12}I_{14} \) — the ground line — and also on \( I_{23}I_{34} \), the coupler line. Extend both and they cross.

\( I_{24} \) is the point that links 2 and 4 share, so it has the same velocity considered as a point of either link. As a point of link 2 that velocity is \( \omega_2 \cdot |O_2I_{24}| \); as a point of link 4 it is \( \omega_4 \cdot |O_4I_{24}| \). Equate them:

Key relation — velocity ratio from an instant centre

\[ \frac{\omega_4}{\omega_2}=\frac{|O_2 I_{24}|}{|O_4 I_{24}|} \]

A ratio of two distances measured off a drawing — no trigonometry, no calculus.

In the figure the coupler line extended crosses the ground line 54.44 mm beyond \( O_2 \), so \( |O_2I_{24}| = 54.44 \) and \( |O_4I_{24}| = 154.44 \) mm. Their ratio is 0.3525, which is \( \omega_4/\omega_2 \) to four decimal places. That agreement is what makes the construction worth knowing: it is an independent check on an analytical result, obtainable in seconds, and the two methods share no arithmetic.

§4 · Why the speed ratio will not hold still

A gear pair has one ratio, fixed by tooth counts. A linkage does not, and the instant-centre picture shows why: \( I_{24} \) is not a fixed point. As the crank turns, the coupler line sweeps and the crossing point slides along the ground line, so the ratio of the two distances — and therefore the output speed — changes continuously. Sweeping the linkage in the figure through a full revolution, \( |\omega_4/\omega_2| \) ranges from 0.0014 at \( \theta_2 = 239^\circ \) to 0.838 at \( 342^\circ \).

The near-zero value is a physical event, not a numerical accident: it is the rocker at the end of its swing, momentarily stopped and about to reverse. Those toggle positions occur when the crank and coupler fall into one line, and their locations follow from the same cosine rule used for position. For this linkage the rocker turns between \( \theta_4 = 49.46^\circ \) and \( 114.62^\circ \) — a swing of 65.17°, which is the specification a designer actually cares about. Between those limits the output slows to a stop and accelerates back, and a mechanism whose output velocity is changing is a mechanism generating inertia forces. That is Lesson 3.

quiz.q:
Position of a four-bar by the cosine rule

Problem. Ground 100 mm, crank 40 mm, coupler 120 mm, rocker 90 mm, with the crank at \( \theta_2 = 60^\circ \) from the ground line. Locate the crank pin A, find the distance \( d \) from A to the fixed pivot \( O_4 \), and solve the open circuit for \( \theta_3 \) and \( \theta_4 \).
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( A = (40\cos 60^\circ,\ 40\sin 60^\circ) = (20.00,\ 34.64)\ \mathrm{mm} \).

(2) \( d = \sqrt{(100-20.00)^2+(0-34.64)^2} = \sqrt{6400+1200} = 87.18\ \mathrm{mm} \). Check assembly: \( |120-90| = 30 \le 87.18 \le 210 \) ✓.

(3) In triangle \( AO_4B \), the angle at \( O_4 \) between \( O_4A \) and \( O_4B \) is \( \gamma \), with \( \cos\gamma = \frac{d^2+r_4^2-r_3^2}{2dr_4} = \frac{7600+8100-14400}{2(87.18)(90)} = 0.08295 \), so \( \gamma = 85.24^\circ \).

(4) The direction from \( O_4 \) to A is \( \operatorname{atan2}(34.64,\ 20.00-100) = 156.59^\circ \). The open circuit takes \( \theta_4 = 156.59^\circ - 85.24^\circ = 71.34^\circ \), giving \( B = (100+90\cos 71.34^\circ,\ 90\sin 71.34^\circ) = (128.80,\ 85.27)\ \mathrm{mm} \).

(5) \( \theta_3 = \operatorname{atan2}(85.27-34.64,\ 128.80-20.00) = 24.95^\circ \).

Answer: \( \theta_3 = 24.95^\circ \), \( \theta_4 = 71.34^\circ \). Sanity check: close the loop numerically — \( |AB| = \sqrt{(128.80-20.00)^2+(85.27-34.64)^2} = 120.000 \) mm and \( |O_4B| = 90.000 \) mm, both exact to three decimals. The crossed circuit, taking \( \theta_4 = 156.59^\circ + 85.24^\circ \), is equally valid algebra and describes a linkage that would have to be dismantled to reach.

quiz.q:
Velocity two ways, and they must agree

Problem. The same linkage runs at \( \omega_2 = 10 \) rad/s counter-clockwise, with \( \theta_3 = 24.95^\circ \) and \( \theta_4 = 71.34^\circ \) from the previous problem. Find \( \omega_3 \) and \( \omega_4 \) analytically, then locate \( I_{24} \) and confirm \( \omega_4 \) from the drawing.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( \omega_3 = \frac{r_2\omega_2\sin(\theta_4-\theta_2)}{r_3\sin(\theta_3-\theta_4)} = \frac{40(10)\sin(11.34^\circ)}{120\sin(-46.39^\circ)} = \frac{78.66}{-86.87} = -0.905\ \mathrm{rad/s} \).

(2) \( \omega_4 = \frac{r_2\omega_2\sin(\theta_2-\theta_3)}{r_4\sin(\theta_4-\theta_3)} = \frac{40(10)\sin(35.05^\circ)}{90\sin(46.39^\circ)} = \frac{229.7}{65.15} = 3.525\ \mathrm{rad/s} \).

(3) \( I_{24} \) lies where the coupler line AB extended meets the ground line \( y=0 \). Parametrising from A to B, \( y \) reaches zero at \( t = \frac{0-34.64}{85.27-34.64} = -0.6842 \), giving \( x = 20.00 - 0.6842(128.80-20.00) = -54.44\ \mathrm{mm} \).

(4) \( |O_2I_{24}| = 54.44 \) mm and \( |O_4I_{24}| = 54.44+100 = 154.44 \) mm, so \( \omega_4/\omega_2 = 54.44/154.44 = 0.3525 \) and \( \omega_4 = 3.525 \) rad/s.

Answer: \( \omega_3 = -0.905 \) rad/s, \( \omega_4 = 3.525 \) rad/s, confirmed by the instant centre. Sanity check: \( I_{24} \) came out negative, meaning it sits outside the linkage on the far side of \( O_2 \) — normal, and the reason instant-centre constructions need generous paper. The two methods share no arithmetic: one is trigonometry on the loop derivative, the other a ratio of two lengths. Agreement to four decimals is therefore a real check, not a restatement.

quiz.q:
Rocker swing and the toggle positions (US customary)

Problem. A crank-rocker has ground 4.0 in, crank 1.6 in, coupler 4.8 in, rocker 3.6 in — the same proportions as the worked linkage, scaled. The rocker reaches its extremes when the crank and coupler line up. Find the two extreme rocker angles and the total swing, and state what the output velocity does there.
quiz.solution:
Solution. At an extreme the crank and coupler are collinear, so the distance \( O_2B \) is either \( r_3+r_2 = 6.4 \) in (crank pointing away) or \( r_3-r_2 = 3.2 \) in (crank folded back). Each case makes a triangle with the ground 4.0 in and the rocker 3.6 in.

(1) Extended: \( \cos\theta_4 = \frac{r_1^2+r_4^2-(r_3+r_2)^2}{2r_1r_4} = \frac{16.00+12.96-40.96}{2(4.0)(3.6)} = \frac{-12.00}{28.8} = -0.4167 \), so \( \theta_4 = 114.62^\circ \).

(2) Folded: \( \cos\theta_4 = \frac{16.00+12.96-10.24}{28.8} = \frac{18.72}{28.8} = 0.6500 \), so \( \theta_4 = 49.46^\circ \).

(3) Swing \( = 114.62^\circ - 49.46^\circ = 65.17^\circ \).

Answer: the rocker swings 65.17°, between 49.46° and 114.62°, and at both limits the output angular velocity is momentarily zero. Sanity check: the angles match the millimetre linkage exactly, as they must — the cosine rule is homogeneous in length, so scaling every link by 0.04 changes no angle. That is also why a linkage can be designed on any convenient scale and manufactured at another. The sweep of the mm version confirms the zero: the minimum of \( |\omega_4/\omega_2| \) over a revolution is 0.0014, found at \( \theta_2 = 239^\circ \), which is a numerical sampling of an exact zero between two sampled degrees.

quiz.q: A four-bar has how many instant centres?
quiz.solution: \( N(N-1)/2 = 4(3)/2 = 6 \) — one for every pair of links, ground included. Four of them are the pin joints, found by inspection; the other two, \( I_{13} \) and \( I_{24} \), have to be constructed with Kennedy's theorem. The count grows quickly: a six-bar has fifteen, which is why the method is used selectively rather than exhaustively.

quiz.q: The Aronhold-Kennedy theorem states that for any three bodies in plane motion, their three instant centres
quiz.solution: They are collinear. That single fact is what makes the construction work: an unknown centre is placed at the crossing of two lines, each drawn through a pair of centres that are already known. For \( I_{24} \) in a four-bar, one line is the ground (from links 1, 2, 4) and the other is the coupler (from links 2, 3, 4).

quiz.q: An analysis returns \( \omega_3 = -0.905 \) rad/s while \( \omega_2 \) is positive. This means
choices: the coupler turns opposite to the crank at that instant
the analysis picked the wrong circuit
the coupler is at a toggle position
quiz.solution: A negative angular velocity is a direction, and in a four-bar the coupler routinely reverses its sense of rotation within one revolution of the crank while the crank keeps turning one way. Nothing is wrong. A wrong circuit would show up in the position solution as a linkage that is a mirror image of the one built, and a toggle shows up as an output velocity passing through zero, not as a sign.

quiz.q: Doubling \( \omega_2 \) with the linkage held at the same crank angle
choices: doubles every angular velocity and leaves the ratios unchanged
quiz.solution: The velocity equations are linear and homogeneous in \( \omega_2 \), so every velocity scales with it while the geometry — and therefore every ratio — is untouched. Quadrupling is the answer for the acceleration terms, which go as \( \omega^2 \); mixing the two up is the most common error in a first dynamic analysis.

quiz.q: Position analysis of a four-bar requires a cosine rule whose argument comes out greater than 1. The correct interpretation is
choices: a rounding error — clamp it to 1
the crossed circuit should be used
the linkage cannot be assembled at that crank angle
the input speed is too high
quiz.solution: The triangle formed by the coupler, the rocker and the distance \( d \) does not exist, so the chain cannot close at that crank angle: the linkage physically cannot occupy that position. It is the Grashof result of Lesson 1 arriving as broken arithmetic, and it happens exactly when \( d \) falls outside \( |r_3-r_4| \) to \( r_3+r_4 \). Clamping the cosine hides a real geometric verdict, and speed has nothing to do with position analysis.

quiz.q: The velocity ratio of a four-bar varies through the cycle because
choices: the input speed is not constant
quiz.solution: The ratio equals \( |O_2I_{24}|/|O_4I_{24}| \), and \( I_{24} \) is the crossing of the coupler line with the ground line. As the crank turns, the coupler sweeps and that crossing slides, so the ratio changes continuously — even with a perfectly constant input speed and perfectly rigid, frictionless links. A gear pair, whose contact line keeps a fixed crossing point, is exactly the opposite case.

quiz.q: At a toggle position of a crank-rocker,
choices: the output angular velocity is momentarily zero
the mechanism gains a degree of freedom
quiz.solution: Toggle is the rocker at the end of its swing: it stops and reverses, so its angular velocity passes through zero while the crank continues at full speed. The crank does not stop — in a Grashof crank-rocker it cannot. The transmission angle at those positions is typically at or near its worst, not 90°, and no degree of freedom appears; that is a different phenomenon belonging to special geometries.

quiz.q: Why is an instant-centre construction worth doing when the analytical solution is already available?
choices: It works for non-Grashof linkages only
It is an independent check that shares no arithmetic with the analysis
quiz.solution: The two routes have nothing in common: one differentiates the loop equation, the other measures two distances on a drawing. When they agree to four decimals, as they do for the worked linkage at 0.3525, a whole class of algebra and sign errors has been eliminated. It is not more accurate — drawing tolerance limits it — and it stops at velocity; accelerations need the polygon method of Lesson 3.

2.kuwait:
Applied case — the conveyor that indexed short. A packaging line used a crank-rocker to index cartons: the rocker's swing set the stroke, and the stroke was specified at 60° of rocker rotation. After a coupler was replaced following a crash, the line ran but cartons crept out of position over a shift, and the fault was blamed on the servo tuning. It was not the servo; the replacement coupler was 5 mm longer than the drawing.

The swing follows from the extreme positions, where the crank and coupler line up. Working the cosine rule at both extremes for the original set — ground 100, crank 40, coupler 120, rocker 90 mm — gives rocker limits of 49.46° and 114.62°, a swing of 65.17°. Nothing in that calculation involves speed, torque or control gains. It is four lengths and two cosine rules, and it is the number the mechanical design promised the controller. A coupler 5 mm long moves both extremes, and the controller, commanding the same crank rotation, delivers a stroke that no longer matches the pitch. The drift per cycle was under a millimetre, which is precisely why it was chased in software for two days.

Two practices follow. The stroke of a linkage is a consequence of four link lengths, so those lengths carry the tolerance that the stroke specification demands — a coupler is not generic bar stock cut to a tape measure. And when a machine's geometry has been disturbed, the first check is the geometry: extreme positions and swing take a minute to compute from the drawing and settle whether the mechanism can still do what the controller is being asked to correct for.
2.recap:
• Position analysis is one idea: walk round the closed chain as vectors and arrive back at the start, \( \sum r_ie^{i\theta_i}=0 \).
  • Solve it as geometry, not algebra — locate the crank pin, measure \( d \) to the far pivot, then two cosine rules finish the triangle.
  • Two roots exist, the open and crossed circuits; a built linkage lives in one and cannot change without being dismantled.
  • A cosine argument outside \( \pm1 \) is not a rounding error — it means the linkage cannot be assembled at that crank angle.
  • Differentiating the loop gives angular velocities linear in \( \omega_2 \): doubling the input doubles every velocity and changes no ratio.
  • A negative \( \omega_3 \) is a direction. The coupler reverses within one crank revolution as a matter of course.
  • A four-bar has \( 4(3)/2 = 6 \) instant centres; four are the pins, and Kennedy's collinearity theorem locates the other two.
  • \( \omega_4/\omega_2 = |O_2I_{24}|/|O_4I_{24}| \) — a velocity ratio read off a drawing, which reproduced the analytical 0.3525 exactly and shares no arithmetic with it.
  • The ratio varies through the cycle because \( I_{24} \) moves; here it runs from 0.0014 to 0.838.
  • Toggle positions — crank in line with coupler — set the rocker extremes (49.46° to 114.62°, a 65.17° swing) and are where the output velocity passes through zero.

3.lecture:
§1 · The derivative that sends the bill

Position tells you whether the parts fit. Velocity tells you how fast the machine runs. It is acceleration that sends the bill, because acceleration is what inertia responds to: every link that is being accelerated pushes back on whatever accelerates it, with \( ma \) at its centre of mass and \( I_G\alpha \) about it. Those reactions travel through the pins into the bearings and the frame, and they are usually far larger than the useful load.

The scale is easy to underestimate. The slider-crank in the figure — a 50 mm crank and a 200 mm rod at 200 rad/s, about 1910 rev/min — puts 2500 m/s² on the piston at top dead centre. A piston of only 0.5 kg then needs 1250 N to accelerate it, 255 times its own weight. Nothing in the machine cares what the piston weighs; everything cares what it is being accelerated to.

Two more consequences follow from the same number. Inertia forces go as \( \omega^2 \), so raising a machine's speed by 20% raises them by 44% — which is why speeding up existing machinery is a structural question, not a motor question. And they reverse direction twice per revolution, so they are a fatigue load, not a static one.

§2 · The slider-crank, exactly and usefully

Put the crank pin at radius \( r \) and the rod at length \( L \). The piston position follows from the closed loop directly, with \( n = L/r \):

\[ x = r\left(\cos\theta + \sqrt{n^2-\sin^2\theta}\,\right) \]

Differentiating twice with respect to time at constant \( \omega \) gives the exact acceleration, and expanding the square root for \( n \gg 1 \) gives the form actually used.

Key relation — piston acceleration

\[ a = -r\omega^2\left[\cos\theta + \frac{n^2\cos 2\theta + \sin^4\theta}{(n^2-\sin^2\theta)^{3/2}}\right] \qquad\longrightarrow\qquad a \approx -r\omega^2\left(\cos\theta + \frac{\cos 2\theta}{n}\right) \]

The first term is the primary component, at crank frequency; the second is the secondary, at twice crank frequency, and it exists only because the rod has finite length. \( n \to \infty \) would delete it.

The approximation is better than it looks. At \( \theta = 0 \) both give \( -r\omega^2(1+1/n) = -2500 \) m/s² exactly; at \( 180^\circ \) both give \( +1500 \) m/s². The largest disagreement over the whole revolution is at \( \theta = 90^\circ \), where the approximation reads 500 against the exact 516.4 m/s² — 3.2% low, and low at the point where the acceleration is small anyway. That is why the two-term form survives in engine practice: it is accurate where the loads are large and only approximate where they are not.

The secondary term is not a rounding detail. Its amplitude is \( 1/n \) of the primary, so at \( n=4 \) it contributes a quarter as much, at twice the frequency — and it is the reason a four-cylinder engine that is perfectly balanced at crank frequency still shakes at twice it. Lesson 10 returns to exactly this term.

§3 · Acceleration of a linkage: the loop, differentiated twice

For a general linkage there is no closed form worth memorising; there is a procedure. Take the velocity equation and differentiate again. Each link contributes two acceleration terms: a centripetal part \( \omega^2 r \) pointing from the moving pin back at the centre of rotation, and a tangential part \( \alpha r \) perpendicular to the link.

Key relation — acceleration difference

\[ \mathbf{a}_B=\mathbf{a}_A+\boldsymbol{\alpha}_3\times\mathbf{r}_{B/A} -\omega_3^2\,\mathbf{r}_{B/A} \]

Everything on the right except \( \alpha_3 \) is known once the velocity analysis is done, so the two scalar components give two linear equations in the two unknown angular accelerations.

Applied to the four-bar of Lesson 2 — ground 100, crank 40, coupler 120, rocker 90 mm, \( \omega_2 = 10 \) rad/s constant, so \( \alpha_2=0 \) — the solution is \( \alpha_3 = 33.05 \) rad/s² and \( \alpha_4 = 39.93 \) rad/s². Note what a constant input speed did not buy: both driven links are accelerating hard. A motor running at perfectly steady speed still generates inertia loads throughout the mechanism, because the mechanism's own geometry keeps changing the ratio, as Lesson 2 showed.

Drawn rather than solved, the same equation is an acceleration polygon: lay the known vectors head to tail, and the two unknown tangential components close the figure. It is the same arithmetic with a ruler, and it has the same virtue as the instant-centre construction — it is an independent check.

§4 · Coriolis, and why it is the term that gets forgotten

Everything above assumed each pair of links keeps a fixed distance. When one link slides along another that is itself rotating — a block in a swinging slot, the shoe of a quick-return, a follower running in a rotating guide — a fifth term appears.

Key relation — Coriolis acceleration

\[ \mathbf{a}_{\text{cor}}=2\,\boldsymbol{\omega}\times\mathbf{v}_{\text{rel}} \]

Present whenever sliding happens on a rotating member; perpendicular to the sliding velocity; zero only if the guide is not rotating or the block is not sliding.

Its size is routinely underestimated. Take a slotted lever turning at \( \omega = 8 \) rad/s with \( \alpha = 12 \) rad/s², carrying a block 0.25 m from the pivot that is sliding outward at 1.5 m/s with 4 m/s² of its own. The four contributions are: centripetal \( \omega^2 r = 16 \), tangential \( \alpha r = 3 \), relative 4, and Coriolis \( 2\omega v = 24 \) m/s². Coriolis is the largest of them — eight times the tangential term. Collecting components along and across the slot gives \( -12 \) and \( +27 \) m/s², a total of 29.5 m/s². Leave Coriolis out and the answer is 12.4 m/s²: 58% low, and 58% low on a bearing load.

The practical rule is to look for the sliding pair first. If any joint in the chain lets one link slide along another that rotates, the term is there, it is perpendicular to the slot, and it is often the dominant one. Quick-return mechanisms, Scotch yokes and swinging-block linkages all carry it.

What this lesson assumes

  • Velocity analysis (Lesson 2) — the acceleration equations are the velocity equations differentiated once more, and reuse their results.
  • Normal and tangential acceleration (Dynamics L2) — \( v^2/\rho \) and \( dv/dt \), reappearing as \( \omega^2r \) and \( \alpha r \).
  • Rotating reference frames (Dynamics L6) — the source of the Coriolis term.
  • Newton's second law (Physics I) — why acceleration, not velocity, sets the force.
  • Binomial expansion (Mathematics I) — expanding \( \sqrt{n^2-\sin^2\theta} \) is what produces the two-term form.

quiz.q:
Piston acceleration, exact against approximate

Problem. A slider-crank has crank \( r = 50 \) mm, connecting rod \( L = 200 \) mm and runs at a constant \( \omega = 200 \) rad/s. Find the piston acceleration at \( \theta = 0^\circ \), \( 90^\circ \) and \( 180^\circ \) using the two-term approximation, and compare with the exact values −2500.00, +516.40 and +1500.00 m/s². State where the approximation is worst.
quiz.solution:
Solution. \( n = L/r = 200/50 = 4 \) and \( r\omega^2 = 0.050(200)^2 = 2000\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \).

(1) \( \theta = 0^\circ \): \( a = -2000\left(\cos 0 + \frac{\cos 0}{4}\right) = -2000(1+0.25) = -2500\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \). Exact value \( -2500.00 \) — error 0.00%.

(2) \( \theta = 90^\circ \): \( a = -2000\left(0 + \frac{-1}{4}\right) = +500\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \). Exact \( +516.40 \) — error \( (500-516.40)/516.40 = -3.18\% \).

(3) \( \theta = 180^\circ \): \( a = -2000\left(-1 + \frac{1}{4}\right) = +1500\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \). Exact \( +1500.00 \) — error 0.00%.

Answer: −2500, +500 and +1500 m/s²; the approximation is worst at \( 90^\circ \), 3.2% low. Sanity check: the errors land where they should. At 0° and 180° the crank and rod are collinear, the geometry is exactly captured by two terms, and the answers are exact. The error appears at 90° — where the acceleration is smallest, so 3.2% of a small number. The peak magnitude is 2500 m/s² at top dead centre, and that is where the approximation has no error at all, which is why it is trusted for sizing.

quiz.q:
Angular accelerations of a four-bar

Problem. The Lesson 2 linkage — ground 100, crank 40, coupler 120, rocker 90 mm — runs at a constant \( \omega_2 = 10 \) rad/s, so \( \alpha_2 = 0 \). At \( \theta_2 = 60^\circ \) the earlier analysis gave \( \theta_3 = 24.95^\circ \), \( \theta_4 = 71.34^\circ \), \( \omega_3 = -0.905 \) and \( \omega_4 = 3.525 \) rad/s. Find \( \alpha_3 \) and \( \alpha_4 \).
quiz.solution:
Solution. Differentiating the loop twice and separating components gives two linear equations in \( \alpha_3, \alpha_4 \). Collecting the known terms:

\( A = r_4\sin\theta_4 = 90\sin 71.34^\circ = 85.27 \); \( B = r_3\sin\theta_3 = 120\sin 24.95^\circ = 50.63 \); \( D = r_4\cos\theta_4 = 28.80 \); \( E = r_3\cos\theta_3 = 108.80 \).

\( C = r_2\omega_2^2\cos\theta_2 + r_3\omega_3^2\cos\theta_3 - r_4\omega_4^2\cos\theta_4 = 2000.0 + 89.15 - 322.10 = 1767.05 \).

\( F = -r_2\omega_2^2\sin\theta_2 - r_3\omega_3^2\sin\theta_3 + r_4\omega_4^2\sin\theta_4 = -3464.10 - 41.48 + 953.65 = -2551.93 \).

\( \alpha_3 = \frac{CD-AF}{AE-BD} = \frac{(1767.05)(28.80) - (85.27)(-2551.93)}{(85.27)(108.80)-(50.63)(28.80)} = \frac{50\,891 + 217\,600}{9277.4-1458.1} = 33.05\ \mathrm{rad/s^2} \).

\( \alpha_4 = \frac{CE-BF}{AE-BD} = \frac{(1767.05)(108.80)-(50.63)(-2551.93)}{7819.3} = \frac{192\,255 + 129\,204}{7819.3} = 39.93\ \mathrm{rad/s^2} \).

Answer: \( \alpha_3 = 33.05 \) rad/s², \( \alpha_4 = 39.93 \) rad/s². Sanity check: differentiating \( \omega_3 \) and \( \omega_4 \) numerically across \( \theta_2 = 60^\circ \) reproduces both to four decimals. The physical reading matters more than the arithmetic: the input shaft is at perfectly constant speed, and the coupler and rocker are still accelerating at 33 and 40 rad/s². Constant input speed does not mean an inertia-free mechanism — the varying velocity ratio of Lesson 2 guarantees the opposite.

quiz.q:
The Coriolis term in a quick-return

Problem. A block slides in the slot of a rotating lever. At the instant of interest the lever turns at \( \omega = 8 \) rad/s with \( \alpha = 12 \) rad/s², and the block is 0.25 m from the pivot, sliding outward along the slot at 1.5 m/s and accelerating along it at 4 m/s². Find the block's total acceleration, and find what it would come to if the Coriolis term were omitted.
quiz.solution:
Solution. Four contributions, resolved along the slot (radial, outward positive) and across it (transverse):

(1) Centripetal \( \omega^2 r = 8^2(0.25) = 16\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \), radial inward.

(2) Tangential \( \alpha r = 12(0.25) = 3\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \), transverse.

(3) Relative \( a_{\text{rel}} = 4\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \), radial outward.

(4) Coriolis \( 2\omega v_{\text{rel}} = 2(8)(1.5) = 24\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \), transverse, in the same sense as the tangential term for outward sliding.

Radial: \( -16 + 4 = -12\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \). Transverse: \( 3 + 24 = 27\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \).

\( a = \sqrt{12^2+27^2} = \sqrt{144+729} = 29.55\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \).

Without Coriolis: transverse \( = 3 \), so \( a = \sqrt{144+9} = 12.37\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \).

Answer: 29.55 m/s²; omitting Coriolis gives 12.37 m/s², 58% low. Sanity check: Coriolis supplies 24 of the 27 m/s² of transverse acceleration — 89% of it, and eight times the tangential term from the lever's own angular acceleration. An error of that size propagates directly into the block's inertia force and the slot's contact pressure, which is why quick-return and swinging-block mechanisms are the classic place to lose a bearing to an analysis that looked complete.

quiz.q: Inertia forces in a machine are sized by
quiz.solution: \( F = ma \) and \( M = I_G\alpha \): it is acceleration that inertia resists. A link can be moving fast and load nothing extra if it is moving at constant velocity in a straight line, and can be momentarily at rest — at a toggle, say — while carrying its largest inertia load. Jerk matters for smoothness and for cam wear, but it does not appear in a force equation.

quiz.q: A machine's speed is raised from 1000 to 1200 rev/min. The inertia forces increase by about
quiz.solution: Inertia forces go as \( \omega^2 \), so the factor is \( (1.2)^2 = 1.44 \) — a 44% increase for a 20% speed rise. This is why "just run it faster" is a structural and bearing question rather than a motor question: the drive may have the power to spare while the pins, the frame and the foundations do not.

quiz.q: In \( a \approx -r\omega^2(\cos\theta + \cos 2\theta/n) \), the second term exists because
choices: the connecting rod has finite length
of friction in the wrist pin
quiz.solution: It is the finite rod ratio \( n = L/r \). An infinitely long rod would keep the piston in pure simple harmonic motion at crank frequency, and the secondary term would vanish. Its amplitude is \( 1/n \) of the primary — a quarter at \( n = 4 \) — and it oscillates at twice crank frequency, which is why it appears as a distinct engine vibration order in Lesson 10.

quiz.q: For a slider-crank at constant \( \omega \), the piston acceleration is largest
quiz.solution: At top dead centre both terms add: \( -r\omega^2(1+1/n) \), which for the worked case is \( -2500 \) m/s², against \( +1500 \) at bottom dead centre where they partly cancel, \( -r\omega^2(-1+1/n) \). The asymmetry between the two ends is entirely the secondary term, and it is why the piston-pin and rod loads at the top of the stroke govern the design.

quiz.q: The Coriolis component is present whenever
choices: a link rotates at constant speed
a point slides along a member that is itself rotating
quiz.solution: \( 2\boldsymbol{\omega}\times\mathbf{v}_{\text{rel}} \) needs both factors: a rotating frame and a sliding velocity within it. A plain pin joint has no relative sliding, so no Coriolis term; a slider on a fixed guide has no rotation, so none either. A block in a swinging slot has both, and there the term is often the largest of the four.

quiz.q: An analysis of a swinging-block mechanism omits the Coriolis term and reports 12.4 m/s² where the true value is 29.5. The consequence is
choices: no consequence — Coriolis affects direction only
the block's inertia force and the slot contact pressure are underestimated by more than half
the velocity analysis must also be wrong
quiz.solution: Acceleration multiplies mass to give force, so a 58% low acceleration is a 58% low inertia force and a correspondingly low contact pressure in the slot — the opposite of conservative. The velocity analysis is unaffected: Coriolis appears only when the velocity result is differentiated, which is exactly why the mistake survives a review that checked the velocities and found them right.

quiz.q: A four-bar is driven at perfectly constant \( \omega_2 \). The angular acceleration of the coupler is
quiz.solution: Constant input speed makes \( \alpha_2 = 0 \) and nothing else. Because the velocity ratio of a linkage changes continuously with position, \( \omega_3 \) and \( \omega_4 \) vary through the cycle and their derivatives are generally non-zero — 33.05 and 39.93 rad/s² for the worked linkage at \( \theta_2 = 60^\circ \). A steady motor does not give an inertia-free mechanism.

quiz.q: The centripetal term \( \omega^2 r \) in an acceleration analysis always points
choices: from the point toward its centre of rotation
perpendicular to the link, in the sense of \( \alpha \)
quiz.solution: It points from the moving point back at the centre it is turning about, which is why it is fully known as soon as the velocity analysis is finished — both its magnitude \( \omega^2r \) and its direction come from results already in hand. The tangential term \( \alpha r \) is the perpendicular one, and it carries the unknown that the acceleration equations are solved for.

3.kuwait:
Applied case — the compressor that failed its pins after an uprate. A reciprocating compressor was run 20% faster to recover throughput after a process change. The drive had the power, the valves were re-selected, and the machine met its new duty. Within a few months the wrist-pin bushes on two cylinders were found spread and the rod small-ends picked up.

Nothing was wrong with the parts. The inertia force on a reciprocating mass goes as \( \omega^2 \), so a 20% speed rise multiplies it by \( 1.2^2 = 1.44 \): every pin in the machine saw 44% more load, on every stroke, forever. Worked in numbers on a comparable geometry — 50 mm crank, 200 mm rod — the peak piston acceleration at top dead centre is \( r\omega^2(1+r/L) \), which at 200 rad/s is 2500 m/s², so a 0.5 kg reciprocating mass already pushes 1250 N through the pin, 255 times its own weight, before any gas load is added. Add 44% and the bearing is running outside the pressure it was selected for while every performance figure on the datasheet still reads correctly.

Two practices follow. A speed change is a re-analysis of the inertia loads, not a control setting: the \( \omega^2 \) law means the machine that is 20% faster is a machine with 44% more load in its running gear. And the inertia load reverses twice per revolution, so it is a fatigue duty — the consequence of getting it wrong is not an immediate failure that would have been caught during commissioning, but a life that has been quietly divided by a large number.
3.recap:
• Acceleration, not velocity, sets inertia loads: \( F=ma \) at the centre of mass and \( M=I_G\alpha \) about it.
  • The scale is large — a 0.5 kg piston at 2500 m/s² pushes 1250 N through its pin, 255 times its own weight.
  • Inertia forces go as \( \omega^2 \): a 20% speed rise means 44% more load, and it reverses twice per revolution, so it is a fatigue duty.
  • Slider-crank exactly: \( a=-r\omega^2\left[\cos\theta+\frac{n^2\cos 2\theta+\sin^4\theta}{(n^2-\sin^2\theta)^{3/2}}\right] \), with \( n=L/r \).
  • Two-term working form \( a \approx -r\omega^2(\cos\theta+\cos 2\theta/n) \): exact at both dead centres, worst error 3.2% at \( 90^\circ \) where the acceleration is small.
  • The secondary term exists only because the rod is finite; its amplitude is \( 1/n \) of the primary and its frequency is twice crank speed.
  • Linkage acceleration is the velocity loop differentiated again: a centripetal \( \omega^2r \) that is already known, plus a tangential \( \alpha r \) that carries the unknown.
  • Constant input speed does not mean zero acceleration elsewhere — the worked four-bar gives \( \alpha_3=33.05 \) and \( \alpha_4=39.93 \) rad/s² at \( \alpha_2=0 \).
  • Coriolis \( 2\omega v_{\text{rel}} \) appears wherever sliding happens on a rotating member, perpendicular to the slot.
  • It is easily the dominant term: in the worked block it was 24 of 27 m/s² transverse, and omitting it gave an answer 58% low.

4.lecture:
§1 · The cam is the motion, written down

A linkage produces the motion its proportions allow. A cam produces the motion you specify: its profile is the displacement schedule, machined into steel. That is the trade — complete freedom over the follower's motion, paid for with a higher pair, line contact, contact stress and wear, in place of the linkage's comfortable pins.

Design starts from the displacement diagram: follower lift against cam angle, laid out as a sequence of rises, dwells and returns that the machine's timing demands. The dwells are usually why the cam was chosen at all — no linkage holds an output perfectly still for a third of a revolution. What has to be decided is what happens during a rise, and that choice is called the motion law.

The lift is a given: 20 mm here, over a rise of \( \beta = 90^\circ \), at 300 rev/min so \( \omega = 31.42 \) rad/s. Every motion law delivers the same 20 mm over the same 90°. They differ entirely in the derivatives, and the derivatives are what break the machine.

§2 · Three laws, and what their derivatives say

Uniform (constant-velocity) motion is the naive answer: divide the lift evenly across the rise, \( v = h\omega/\beta = 0.400 \) m/s throughout. Its acceleration is zero in the middle and infinite at both ends, where the follower is asked to reach full speed instantly. It exists in practice only with its corners rounded, which means it is not really this law at all.

Simple harmonic motion, \( s=\tfrac{h}{2}\left(1-\cos\frac{\pi\theta}{\beta}\right) \), is the sine wave's projection and is smooth in the middle. Cycloidal motion, \( s=h\left(\frac{\theta}{\beta}-\frac{1}{2\pi}\sin\frac{2\pi\theta}{\beta}\right) \), is a constant-magnitude acceleration vector rotating at constant speed, projected on the axis.

Key relations — peak velocity and acceleration

\[ \text{SHM:}\quad v_{\max}=\frac{\pi h\omega}{2\beta},\qquad a_{\max}=\frac{\pi^2h\omega^2}{2\beta^2} \]

\[ \text{Cycloidal:}\quad v_{\max}=\frac{2h\omega}{\beta},\qquad a_{\max}=\frac{2\pi h\omega^2}{\beta^2} \]

Both cycloidal peaks are exactly \( 4/\pi = 1.273 \) times the harmonic ones, for any lift, any rise angle and any speed.

For the worked cam: harmonic gives 0.628 m/s and 39.48 m/s²; cycloidal gives 0.800 m/s and 50.26 m/s². On peak numbers alone the harmonic law wins, and at low speed it is chosen for exactly that reason.

§3 · Why cycloidal wins anyway, and what wear tells you

Look at the ends of the rise rather than the middle. Harmonic acceleration begins at \( +39.48 \) m/s² the instant the rise starts — a step, from the zero of the preceding dwell. A step in acceleration is infinite jerk, \( da/dt \). No real follower train is infinitely stiff, so it responds to that step by ringing: the follower, its spring and its linkage form a spring-mass system, and a step excites every mode it has. The result is vibration, noise, and contact stress well above the value the steady analysis predicted.

Cycloidal acceleration leaves zero smoothly and returns to zero smoothly. Its jerk is finite everywhere. It pays 27% more peak acceleration — a quantity that can simply be designed for — to eliminate a quantity that cannot. Above a few hundred rev/min, that is not a close decision.

The exchange shows in wear. A cam cut to a harmonic law and run fast wears in two narrow bands at the ends of the rise, where the step lands and the follower hammers. A cycloidal cam of the same duty wears more evenly and most at mid-rise, where its acceleration and hence its contact force genuinely peak. A worn cam is a record of its own acceleration history, and reading that record is a legitimate diagnostic: bands at the transitions mean the motion law, or its manufacture, has a discontinuity in it.

§4 · Pressure angle, base circle, and keeping the follower on the cam

The cam pushes the follower along the contact normal, which is not the direction the follower moves. The angle between them is the pressure angle \( \phi \), and it does to a cam what the transmission angle does to a linkage.

Key relation — pressure angle, radial roller follower

\[ \tan\phi=\frac{ds/d\theta}{R_p+s} \]

\( R_p \) is the prime-circle radius and \( s \) the lift at that instant. Practice keeps \( \phi \le 30^\circ \) on a translating follower.

The numerator belongs to the motion law and the denominator to the cam's size. Harmonic motion on this cam has \( ds/d\theta = \pi h/2\beta = 20 \) mm/rad at mid-rise, so with \( R_p = 40 \) mm and \( s = 10 \) mm, \( \phi = 21.8^\circ \) — comfortable. Shrink the prime circle to 25 mm and \( \phi = 29.7^\circ \), on the limit. Grow it to 60 mm and \( \phi = 15.9^\circ \). The base circle is the pressure-angle control, and a cam that is too small is the usual cause of a cam that jams. Cycloidal motion, with its steeper mid-rise \( ds/d\theta = 2h/\beta = 25.5 \) mm/rad, gives \( \phi = 27.0^\circ \) on the same 40 mm prime circle — the same trade as before, appearing in a second place.

One more check closes the design. The cam can only push; the follower is returned by a spring, and the spring must hold contact through the whole negative-acceleration phase or the follower lifts off and lands again — follower jump, which destroys cams. The requirement is \( F_{\text{spring}} \ge m\,a_{\max} \) with margin. A 1.2 kg follower on the cycloidal law needs \( 1.2 \times 50.26 = 60.3 \) N at the worst point, so a spring giving about 78 N there carries a 30% margin. Note that the harmonic law would have needed only 47.4 N: the 27% acceleration penalty is paid twice, once in contact stress and once in the spring that has to be carried against it for the whole life of the machine.

quiz.q:
Harmonic against cycloidal, same duty

Problem. A cam lifts a follower 20 mm over a 90° rise and runs at 300 rev/min. Find the peak velocity and peak acceleration for simple harmonic motion and for cycloidal motion, and state the ratio between them.
quiz.solution:
Solution. \( \omega = 2\pi(300)/60 = 31.416 \) rad/s, \( \beta = 90^\circ = \pi/2 = 1.5708 \) rad, \( h = 0.020 \) m.

(1) SHM: \( v_{\max} = \frac{\pi h\omega}{2\beta} = \frac{\pi(0.020)(31.416)}{2(1.5708)} = \frac{1.9739}{3.1416} = 0.628\ \mathrm{m/s} \).

(2) SHM: \( a_{\max} = \frac{\pi^2h\omega^2}{2\beta^2} = \frac{9.8696(0.020)(987.0)}{2(2.4674)} = \frac{194.82}{4.9348} = 39.48\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \).

(3) Cycloidal: \( v_{\max} = \frac{2h\omega}{\beta} = \frac{2(0.020)(31.416)}{1.5708} = 0.800\ \mathrm{m/s} \).

(4) Cycloidal: \( a_{\max} = \frac{2\pi h\omega^2}{\beta^2} = \frac{6.2832(0.020)(987.0)}{2.4674} = \frac{124.02}{2.4674} = 50.26\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \).

Answer: SHM 0.628 m/s and 39.48 m/s²; cycloidal 0.800 m/s and 50.26 m/s²; both cycloidal peaks are \( 4/\pi = 1.273 \) times the harmonic ones. Sanity check: the ratio is exactly \( 4/\pi \) in both velocity and acceleration, and it is independent of \( h \), \( \beta \) and \( \omega \) — the constants cancel. That is worth remembering as a design fact: choosing cycloidal over harmonic always costs 27%, never more, and buys finite jerk. For reference, uniform motion would give the lowest peak velocity of all, \( h\omega/\beta = 0.400 \) m/s, and infinite acceleration at both ends.

quiz.q:
Pressure angle and the base circle

Problem. The cam above uses a radial translating roller follower on a prime circle of radius \( R_p = 40 \) mm, with harmonic motion. Find the pressure angle at mid-rise, where \( ds/d\theta \) is greatest and the lift is \( h/2 \). Then find what \( R_p = 25 \) mm and \( R_p = 60 \) mm would give, and say which designs are acceptable.
quiz.solution:
Solution. For SHM the slope peaks at mid-rise: \( ds/d\theta = \frac{\pi h}{2\beta} = \frac{\pi(20)}{2(1.5708)} = 20.0\ \mathrm{mm/rad} \), and there \( s = h/2 = 10 \) mm.

(1) \( R_p = 40 \): \( \tan\phi = \frac{20.0}{40+10} = 0.4000 \), so \( \phi = 21.80^\circ \) ✓.

(2) \( R_p = 25 \): \( \tan\phi = \frac{20.0}{25+10} = 0.5714 \), so \( \phi = 29.74^\circ \) — on the 30° limit.

(3) \( R_p = 60 \): \( \tan\phi = \frac{20.0}{60+10} = 0.2857 \), so \( \phi = 15.95^\circ \) ✓.

Answer: 21.8°, 29.7° and 16.0°; the 40 and 60 mm cams are comfortable and the 25 mm cam is at the limit with nothing in hand. Sanity check: the motion law appears only in the numerator and the cam size only in the denominator, so the two are independent controls. Switching this cam to cycloidal motion raises the slope to \( 2h/\beta = 25.5 \) mm/rad and, on the 40 mm prime circle, the pressure angle to 27.0° — still acceptable, but the 27% penalty has now appeared in a second place. The general fix for a high pressure angle is a bigger cam, which is also the general reason cams are larger than a first sketch suggests.

quiz.q:
Spring sizing against follower jump (with a US customary check)

Problem. The follower assembly on the cycloidal cam weighs 1.2 kg. Find the spring force needed at the worst point to keep contact, apply a 30% margin, and convert the result to pounds-force. Then state what happens if the spring is 40 N instead.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The cam can only push, so the spring alone supplies the force during the negative-acceleration phase. The requirement is \( F \ge m\,a_{\max} = 1.2(50.26) = 60.3\ \mathrm{N} \).

(2) With a 30% margin, \( F = 1.3(60.3) = 78.4\ \mathrm{N} \).

(3) \( 78.4\ \mathrm{N} \times \frac{1\ \mathrm{lbf}}{4.448\ \mathrm{N}} = 17.6\ \mathrm{lbf} \).

(4) With 40 N the spring can decelerate only \( a = 40/1.2 = 33.3\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \), well short of the 50.26 the cam demands. The follower leaves the cam surface, flies for part of the cycle, and lands on the profile with an impact the design never accounted for.

Answer: 78.4 N (17.6 lbf); a 40 N spring allows follower jump. Sanity check: the same follower on the harmonic law would need only \( 1.2(39.48) = 47.4 \) N before margin, so the 40 N spring would still be marginal but far closer. Two consequences worth naming: the jump condition scales as \( \omega^2 \), so a cam that is safe at 300 rev/min is not automatically safe at 400; and the spring is not a return device that can be sized by feel — it is the component holding a higher pair together.

quiz.q: Cycloidal motion is preferred over simple harmonic for high-speed cams because
choices: its acceleration is continuous at the ends of the rise, so the jerk is finite
quiz.solution: Cycloidal acceleration starts and ends at zero, so there is no step and the jerk stays finite. Harmonic acceleration steps from zero to its peak the instant the rise begins, which is infinite jerk and excites every mode of the follower train. Cycloidal is worse on both peaks — velocity and acceleration are each \( 4/\pi \) times the harmonic values — and needs a larger cam for the same pressure angle. It wins on the derivative that cannot be designed around.

quiz.q: For the same lift, rise angle and speed, the cycloidal peak acceleration exceeds the harmonic by a factor of
quiz.solution: \( \frac{2\pi h\omega^2/\beta^2}{\pi^2h\omega^2/2\beta^2} = \frac{4}{\pi} = 1.273 \). Every parameter cancels, so the 27% penalty is a property of the two motion laws and nothing else — it does not shrink at low lift or long rise. The same factor governs the peak velocities.

quiz.q: Uniform (constant-velocity) follower motion is unusable in its pure form because
choices: the acceleration is infinite at both ends of the rise
the pressure angle is always too large
quiz.solution: Constant velocity means the follower must reach full speed instantly at the start and stop instantly at the end: an acceleration step of infinite height, and therefore an infinite inertia force. In practice the transitions are blended with arcs or a smooth law, which is really a different motion law with a constant-velocity segment in the middle. Its peak velocity is actually the lowest of the three laws, at \( h\omega/\beta \).

quiz.q: A cam has a pressure angle of 34° at mid-rise. The most direct fix is to
choices: use a flat-faced follower and keep the same size
quiz.solution: \( \tan\phi = (ds/d\theta)/(R_p+s) \): the cam's size is the denominator, so enlarging the prime circle lowers the angle directly — the worked cam drops from 29.7° to 16.0° going from a 25 to a 60 mm prime circle. Speed does not appear in the formula at all. A flat-faced follower does sidestep the pressure angle, but it changes the contact geometry and brings its own curvature constraint, so it is a redesign rather than the direct fix.

quiz.q: Follower jump occurs when
choices: the spring force is less than the follower's inertia force during deceleration
the cam runs below its design speed
quiz.solution: A cam can only push. Through the negative-acceleration phase the spring is the only thing decelerating the follower, so it must supply at least \( ma_{\max} \) — 60.3 N for a 1.2 kg follower at 50.26 m/s². Below that the follower separates and returns as an impact. Because the requirement scales with \( \omega^2 \), jump appears when a machine is sped up, never when it is slowed down.

quiz.q: A cam is found worn in two narrow bands at the start and end of its rise, with the mid-rise region comparatively unmarked. This points to
choices: a motion law with an acceleration discontinuity there
a pressure angle problem at mid-rise
quiz.solution: Wear follows contact force, and contact force follows acceleration. Bands at the transitions rather than at mid-rise say the load is spiking where the acceleration steps — the signature of a harmonic or uniform law run too fast, or of a manufacturing discontinuity at the blend. A pressure-angle problem or excessive spring force would show as heavier, broader wear where the pressure angle or the lift peaks, which is mid-rise.

quiz.q: The same cam and follower are run at 400 rev/min instead of 300. The spring force needed to prevent jump increases by a factor of about
quiz.solution: Peak acceleration goes as \( \omega^2 \), so the factor is \( (400/300)^2 = 1.78 \). The 60.3 N requirement becomes 107 N, and the 78.4 N spring chosen with a 30% margin at 300 rev/min is now below the bare minimum. Speed increases on cam-driven machinery have to be checked against the jump condition before anything else.

quiz.q: The dwell is usually the reason a cam is chosen rather than a linkage because
choices: a linkage cannot hold an output exactly stationary for a finite interval
quiz.solution: A linkage output passes through zero velocity instantaneously at a toggle, but it does not stay there; holding a follower genuinely still for a specified arc of the cycle is what a cam does and a four-bar cannot. The price is the higher pair — line contact, high contact stress and wear — where the linkage enjoys surface contact at every joint.

4.kuwait:
Applied case — the filling machine that got faster. A rotary filling machine used a cam to raise each container against the filling head, hold it through the fill, and lower it. Throughput was raised by running the cam shaft from 300 to 400 rev/min, with no other change: the fill volume was corrected in software and the machine passed its trials. Within weeks the cam began showing bright bands and pitting at the two ends of the rise, and containers were occasionally being struck rather than lifted.

Two things changed at once, and both scale as \( \omega^2 \). The peak follower acceleration on this cam's cycloidal rise, \( 2\pi h\omega^2/\beta^2 \), rose by \( (400/300)^2 = 1.78 \) — from 50.3 to 89.4 m/s² — so the 1.2 kg follower assembly now needed \( 1.2 \times 89.4 = 107 \) N to stay on the cam, against a spring chosen to deliver about 78 N. The follower was leaving the profile during the deceleration and landing on it, which is precisely what produces localised bands rather than distributed wear, and what turns a controlled lift into an impact.

Two practices follow. A cam machine's speed is limited by its spring at least as often as by its motor, and the jump check — \( F_{\text{spring}} \ge ma_{\max} \) with margin — must be repeated at the new speed before a rate increase is accepted. And wear patterns are evidence: bands at the transitions of a rise say the follower is losing and regaining contact there, which is a different failure from the even wear of an honestly loaded cam and calls for a different fix.
4.recap:
• A cam's profile is its displacement schedule made physical: complete freedom over the follower's motion, bought with a higher pair and its contact stress.
  • Dwells are usually why a cam is chosen — no linkage holds an output exactly still for a finite part of the cycle.
  • Every motion law delivers the same lift over the same rise; they differ only in the derivatives, and the derivatives break the machine.
  • Uniform motion has the lowest peak velocity, \( h\omega/\beta \), and infinite acceleration at both ends — unusable in pure form.
  • SHM: \( v_{\max}=\pi h\omega/2\beta \), \( a_{\max}=\pi^2h\omega^2/2\beta^2 \) — 0.628 m/s and 39.48 m/s² for the worked cam.
  • Cycloidal: \( v_{\max}=2h\omega/\beta \), \( a_{\max}=2\pi h\omega^2/\beta^2 \) — 0.800 m/s and 50.26 m/s², exactly \( 4/\pi \) times the harmonic values, always.
  • Cycloidal still wins at speed: harmonic acceleration steps at both ends of the rise, which is infinite jerk and rings the follower train.
  • Wear records the acceleration history — bands at the transitions indicate a discontinuity, even wear at mid-rise indicates an honest load.
  • Pressure angle \( \tan\phi = (ds/d\theta)/(R_p+s) \), kept below about 30°; the base circle is its control (29.7° at \( R_p=25 \) mm falls to 16.0° at 60 mm).
  • The spring holds the higher pair together: \( F \ge ma_{\max} \), 78 N with margin here, and the requirement grows as \( \omega^2 \) whenever the machine is sped up.

5.lecture:
§1 · Conjugate action, and the one curve that delivers it

A gear pair has one job that a friction wheel cannot do reliably: hold an exact, constant speed ratio while transmitting torque. Constant means constant through the mesh, not on average — a ratio that fluctuates within a tooth pitch is a vibration source, and it will be found in the spectrum of Lesson 6.

The condition is geometric. Where two tooth flanks touch, the common normal to both surfaces must pass through a fixed point on the line of centres — the pitch point. That is the law of gearing, and any pair of profiles satisfying it is called conjugate. Many curves can be made conjugate to some mate; only one is conjugate to itself, so that a gear cut with it meshes correctly with any other gear of the same pressure angle and pitch. That curve is the involute: the path traced by a point on a taut string unwound from a circle — the base circle.

The involute's decisive property follows from that construction. The string is always tangent to the base circle, so the contact normal always lies along one fixed straight line, the line of action, inclined to the common tangent by the pressure angle \( \phi \). The direction in which one tooth pushes another never changes through the mesh, which means the bearing load direction never changes either. A cycloidal tooth is conjugate too, and does not have that property.

§2 · Module, pitch and the standard tooth

Two gears mesh only if their teeth are the same size, so tooth size is standardised as the module \( m \), the pitch diameter per tooth.

Key relations — gear geometry

\[ m=\frac{d}{N},\qquad p=\pi m,\qquad d_b=d\cos\phi,\qquad C=\frac{m(N_1+N_2)}{2} \]

\( p \) is the circular pitch measured on the pitch circle and \( d_b \) is the base-circle diameter. In US customary practice the same idea is inverted as diametral pitch \( P=N/d \) teeth per inch, with \( m = 25.4/P \) mm.

Take \( m=4 \) mm, \( \phi=20^\circ \), a 20-tooth pinion driving a 40-tooth gear. Then \( d_1 = 80 \), \( d_2 = 160 \) and \( C = 120 \) mm; the base circles are \( 80\cos 20^\circ = 75.18 \) and \( 150.35 \) mm; the circular pitch is \( \pi(4) = 12.566 \) mm and the base pitch \( \pi m\cos\phi = 11.809 \) mm. The standard full-depth tooth then adds an addendum of \( 1m \) above the pitch circle and a dedendum of \( 1.25m \) below it, the extra quarter-module giving root clearance.

§3 · Contact ratio: how many teeth are actually working

Contact begins where the addendum circle of the driven gear cuts the line of action and ends where the driver's addendum circle cuts it. The length between is the length of action \( Z \), and dividing it by the base pitch counts how many tooth pairs are in mesh on average.

Key relation — contact ratio

\[ m_c=\frac{Z}{p_b} =\frac{\sqrt{r_{a1}^2-r_{b1}^2}+\sqrt{r_{a2}^2-r_{b2}^2}-C\sin\phi}{\pi m\cos\phi} \]

\( m_c > 1 \) is mandatory — below it, one pair disengages before the next takes over and the drive stops. Practice wants at least 1.2, and 1.4 or more for quiet running.

For the worked pair, \( \sqrt{44^2-37.588^2}=22.873 \), \( \sqrt{84^2-75.175^2}=37.479 \) and \( C\sin\phi = 41.042 \) mm, so \( Z = 19.309 \) mm and \( m_c = 19.309/11.809 = 1.635 \). Read that as: for 63.5% of the time two tooth pairs share the load, and for the rest a single pair carries everything. It is the fractional part that matters. As the second pair engages and disengages the stiffness of the mesh changes abruptly, and that stiffness variation — not the tooth force itself — is the origin of gear-mesh vibration.

§4 · Interference, and what centre distance does not change

The involute exists only outside the base circle; inside it there is no involute to be conjugate with. If a gear's addendum reaches the mating pinion's flank below its base circle, the tip does not roll — it digs, cutting material out of the pinion's root and leaving it weakened. This is interference, and it is worst for a small pinion driven by a large gear.

Key relation — interference limit

\[ N_{\min}=\frac{2k}{\sin^2\phi} \]

\( k=1 \) for a standard full-depth tooth. This is the limit against a rack, the worst case.

The numbers explain a century of standards work. At \( \phi=14.5^\circ \), \( N_{\min}=31.9 \), so a pinion needed 32 teeth — large gears, large centre distances, modest ratios per stage. At \( 20^\circ \), \( N_{\min}=17.1 \) and an 18-tooth pinion is legal. At \( 25^\circ \) it falls to 11.2, which is why high-ratio and compact drives use the steeper angle, accepting higher radial bearing loads and a lower contact ratio in exchange. When a smaller pinion is unavoidable, the cure is profile shift: cut the tooth with the hob withdrawn slightly, which moves the working part of the flank away from the base circle without changing the module or the mating gear.

Finally, the property that makes involute gears manufacturable at all. Move the gears apart and the pitch circles and pressure angle both change — but the base circles do not, because they were cut into the metal. The line of action still runs tangent to the same two base circles, so the speed ratio is still exactly \( N_1/N_2 \). Opening the worked pair by 1 mm raises the operating pressure angle from 20° to 21.26° and drops the contact ratio from 1.635 to 1.395 — a 14.7% loss of overlap — and opens a backlash of \( 2\Delta C\tan\phi = 0.73 \) mm. The ratio, however, is untouched. A tolerance on centre distance is therefore a tolerance on smoothness and noise, not on kinematic accuracy, which is exactly the trade a housing designer needs to know. Some backlash is required in any case, for lubricant and thermal growth; the design task is to control it, not to eliminate it.
