Interference limit\( N_{\min}=2k/\sin^2\phi \)Smallest legal pinion; 17.1 at 20°.
Profile shifthob withdrawn by \( xm \)Legalising a pinion below \( N_{\min} \).
Backlash\( B \approx 2\Delta C\tan\phi \)Consequence of opening the centre distance.

quiz.q:
Geometry and contact ratio of a gear pair

Problem. A 20-tooth pinion drives a 40-tooth gear, module 4 mm, pressure angle 20°, standard full-depth teeth (addendum \( 1m \)). Find the pitch diameters, centre distance, base-circle radii, base pitch and contact ratio.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( d_1 = mN_1 = 4(20) = 80 \) mm and \( d_2 = 4(40) = 160 \) mm, so \( r_1 = 40 \), \( r_2 = 80 \) and \( C = 40+80 = 120 \) mm.

(2) \( r_{b} = r\cos\phi \): \( r_{b1} = 40\cos 20^\circ = 37.588 \) mm and \( r_{b2} = 75.175 \) mm.

(3) Addendum radii \( r_{a1} = 40+4 = 44 \) mm, \( r_{a2} = 80+4 = 84 \) mm.

(4) \( p_b = \pi m\cos\phi = \pi(4)(0.93969) = 11.809 \) mm.

(5) \( Z = \sqrt{44^2-37.588^2} + \sqrt{84^2-75.175^2} - 120\sin 20^\circ = 22.873 + 37.479 - 41.042 = 19.309 \) mm.

(6) \( m_c = 19.309/11.809 = 1.635 \).

Answer: \( d_1=80 \), \( d_2=160 \), \( C=120 \) mm; \( r_{b1}=37.59 \), \( r_{b2}=75.18 \) mm; \( p_b = 11.81 \) mm; \( m_c = 1.635 \). Sanity check: \( m_c \) comfortably exceeds 1, so the drive never runs out of contact, and its fractional part says two pairs share the load 63.5% of the time and one pair carries everything for the remaining 36.5%. The single-pair interval is the one that sizes the tooth. As an independent check on the arithmetic, \( Z \) must be smaller than \( C\sin\phi = 41.04 \) mm, the whole tangent length between the base circles — and 19.31 mm is 47% of it, which is typical for standard teeth.

quiz.q:
Interference and the choice of pressure angle

Problem. Find the minimum pinion tooth count against a rack for standard full-depth teeth at 14.5°, 20° and 25°. A drive needs a 14-tooth pinion. State which options make that legal and what each costs.
quiz.solution:
Solution. \( N_{\min}=2k/\sin^2\phi \) with \( k=1 \).

(1) \( \phi=14.5^\circ \): \( \sin\phi = 0.25038 \), \( N_{\min} = 2/0.062690 = 31.90 \) → 32 teeth.

(2) \( \phi=20^\circ \): \( \sin\phi = 0.34202 \), \( N_{\min} = 2/0.116978 = 17.10 \) → 18 teeth.

(3) \( \phi=25^\circ \): \( \sin\phi = 0.42262 \), \( N_{\min} = 2/0.178606 = 11.20 \) → 12 teeth.

(4) A 14-tooth pinion is illegal at 20° and legal at 25°. The alternatives are to cut it at 20° with a positive profile shift, or to reduce the addendum (lower \( k \)), since \( N_{\min} \) is proportional to \( k \).

Answer: 32, 18 and 12 teeth; a 14-tooth pinion needs 25°, a profile shift, or a stub tooth. Sanity check: each route has a price. Going to 25° raises the radial component of the tooth force by \( \tan 25^\circ/\tan 20^\circ = 1.28 \), a 28% increase in the separating load the bearings carry, and lowers the contact ratio. A profile shift keeps the module and the mating gear but changes the tooth thickness and needs the pair designed together. A stub tooth reduces the contact ratio directly, since a shorter addendum shortens the length of action. The inverse-square dependence on \( \sin\phi \) is what makes the 14.5° standard so restrictive, and why it was retired.

quiz.q:
Centre-distance error, and a US customary pair

Problem. (a) The 20/40-tooth pair above is assembled with its centres 121 mm apart instead of 120. Find the operating pressure angle, the new contact ratio and the backlash, and say what happens to the speed ratio. (b) Separately, find the contact ratio of an 18/36-tooth pair of diametral pitch 6 per inch at 20°.
quiz.solution:
Solution (a). (1) The base circles are cut into the metal and cannot change, so \( C\cos\phi \) is invariant: \( \cos\phi' = \frac{120\cos 20^\circ}{121} = \frac{112.763}{121} = 0.93192 \), giving \( \phi' = 21.26^\circ \).

(2) The two square-root terms are properties of the gears alone and are unchanged at 22.873 and 37.479 mm, so \( Z' = 22.873+37.479-121\sin 21.26^\circ = 60.352-43.881 = 16.471 \) mm.

(3) \( m_c' = 16.471/11.809 = 1.395 \), down from 1.635 — a 14.7% loss.

(4) \( B \approx 2\Delta C\tan\phi = 2(1)(0.36397) = 0.73 \) mm.

(5) The speed ratio is still exactly \( 40/20 = 2 \), because it is set by the base circles.

Solution (b). \( d_1 = 18/6 = 3.000 \) in, \( d_2 = 6.000 \) in, \( C = 4.500 \) in; \( r_{b1} = 1.5\cos 20^\circ = 1.40954 \), \( r_{b2} = 2.81908 \) in; addendum \( 1/P = 0.16667 \) in so \( r_{a1} = 1.66667 \), \( r_{a2} = 3.16667 \) in; \( p_b = (\pi/6)\cos 20^\circ = 0.49202 \) in. \( Z = 0.88937+1.44242-1.53909 = 0.79270 \) in, so \( m_c = 1.611 \).

Answer: (a) \( \phi'=21.26^\circ \), \( m_c=1.395 \), backlash 0.73 mm, ratio unchanged at 2:1. (b) \( m_c = 1.611 \). Sanity check: part (a) is the practical reason involute teeth won: a housing bore tolerance degrades smoothness and adds backlash but cannot introduce a ratio error, so a gearbox does not need a precision centre distance to keep time. Part (b) confirms the unit system is cosmetic — \( P=6 \) per inch is \( m = 25.4/6 = 4.233 \) mm, close to the 4 mm pair, and the contact ratio comes out at 1.611 against 1.635, the small difference coming from 18 and 36 teeth rather than 20 and 40.

quiz.q: Conjugate action requires that the common normal at the point of tooth contact
choices: be perpendicular to the line of centres
pass through a fixed pitch point on the line of centres
pass through the base circle centre
quiz.solution: That is the law of gearing, and it is what makes the angular-velocity ratio constant instant by instant rather than merely on average. The involute satisfies it by keeping the contact normal along one fixed straight line, the line of action, tangent to both base circles — so the direction of the tooth force, and hence of the bearing load, never changes through the mesh.

quiz.q: Two gears will mesh correctly only if they share the same
quiz.solution: Module fixes tooth size and pressure angle fixes the flank shape, so any two involute gears with both in common will mesh — the involute is conjugate to itself, which is precisely why gears are stocked as catalogue items rather than cut in matched pairs. Tooth counts set the ratio and must differ for a reduction. Face width and material affect capacity, not whether the teeth engage.

quiz.q: A gear pair is computed to have a contact ratio of 0.94. This means
choices: one tooth pair leaves contact before the next enters, so the drive is not continuous
two pairs are always in contact
quiz.solution: A contact ratio below 1 means there are instants with no tooth pair in contact at all: the drive breaks and re-engages every pitch, which is an impact load and, in the strict sense, not a gear drive. Above 1 the mesh is continuous, and the fractional part gives the proportion of time a second pair is sharing the load — 63.5% for the worked pair at 1.635. Practice wants at least 1.2, and more for quiet running.

quiz.q: Interference in a gear pair physically
choices: gouges material from the pinion flank below its base circle, weakening the root
quiz.solution: There is no involute inside the base circle, so a mating tip that reaches below it cannot roll conjugately — it digs. In cutting this shows as undercutting by the hob, which thins the tooth root exactly where the bending stress is highest; in a running pair it shows as scoring. It is avoided by keeping the pinion above \( 2k/\sin^2\phi \) teeth, by profile shift, or by a shorter addendum.

quiz.q: Moving to a 25° pressure angle from 20° allows a smaller pinion. The principal penalty is
choices: a higher radial separating force on the bearings and a lower contact ratio
quiz.solution: The tooth force acts along the line of action, so its radial component goes as \( \tan\phi \): moving from 20° to 25° raises the separating load by \( \tan 25^\circ/\tan 20^\circ = 1.28 \), a 28% increase carried by the bearings and the shafts. The length of action also shortens relative to the base pitch, so the contact ratio falls and the mesh runs less smoothly. The ratio and the module are untouched — those depend on tooth counts and tooth size.

quiz.q: A gearbox housing is bored 1 mm wide, opening a 120 mm centre distance to 121 mm. The speed ratio
choices: is unchanged, because it is set by the base circles
quiz.solution: The base circles were cut into the metal and do not move, and the line of action stays tangent to both, so the ratio remains exactly \( N_2/N_1 \). What does change is the operating pressure angle (20° to 21.26° here), the contact ratio (1.635 to 1.395) and the backlash (0.73 mm). That insensitivity of ratio to centre distance is the involute's great manufacturing advantage.

quiz.q: Backlash in a gear pair is
choices: always a defect to be eliminated
necessary for lubricant film and thermal growth, and controlled rather than removed
the same as the contact ratio
quiz.solution: Zero backlash means the teeth are pinched: no room for an oil film, no room for the housing and gears to grow at different rates, and a jammed drive at temperature. Some is therefore designed in, by tooth-thickness allowance or by centre distance, and specified with a tolerance. It matters most in reversing and positioning drives, where the lost motion at reversal is the backlash, and there it is minimised with anti-backlash arrangements rather than by removing the clearance.

quiz.q: Pure rolling between two involute teeth occurs
choices: nowhere — the contact is pure sliding
quiz.solution: At the pitch point the two flanks have equal velocities, so there is rolling alone; that point is the instant centre of the two gears. Away from it the contact slides, with the sliding velocity growing toward tip and root. That is why scuffing and pitting appear on the flanks above and below the pitch line rather than on it, and why the pitch line is often the last polished band on a worn tooth.

5.kuwait:
Applied case — the replacement pinion that would not run quietly. A drive pinion was replaced on a gearbox after a bearing failure. The new pinion had the correct tooth count and the correct module, the gears meshed, and the ratio was verified on the shafts. The unit ran, but noisily, and a vibration survey found a strong component at tooth-passing frequency that had not been there before.

The pinion had been supplied at 25° pressure angle in place of the original 20°. Nothing in a quick check catches this: module and tooth count fix the pitch diameters, so the centre distance still fits and the shafts still turn at the right ratio. What changes is the flank shape. Two gears of different pressure angle are not conjugate to each other, so contact no longer holds a fixed line of action, the ratio fluctuates within each pitch, and the fluctuation appears exactly at tooth-passing frequency. The steeper pinion also raises the radial separating force by \( \tan 25^\circ/\tan 20^\circ = 1.28 \), which is 28% more load into the bearing that had just been replaced.

Two practices follow. Pressure angle belongs on the spares specification alongside module and tooth count — three numbers, not two, and the third is the one that cannot be measured with a caliper on the shop floor. And a noise complaint that arrives with a new component is a geometry question first: a spectrum peaking at tooth-passing frequency points at the mesh itself, not at the bearings, and the mesh is defined by the pair's shared geometry rather than by either gear alone.
5.recap:
• The law of gearing: the contact normal must pass through a fixed pitch point on the line of centres. Profiles that satisfy it are conjugate.
  • The involute is conjugate to itself, so any two involute gears of the same module and pressure angle mesh — which is why gears are catalogue items.
  • Its contact normal stays on one fixed line of action tangent to both base circles, so the tooth-force direction never changes through the mesh.
  • \( m=d/N \), \( p=\pi m \), \( d_b=d\cos\phi \), \( C=m(N_1+N_2)/2 \); US customary uses \( P=N/d \) with \( m=25.4/P \).
  • Contact ratio \( m_c=Z/p_b \) must exceed 1; the worked 20/40 pair at module 4 gives \( Z=19.31 \) mm, \( p_b=11.81 \) mm and \( m_c=1.635 \).
  • The fractional part is the physics: two pairs share the load 63.5% of the time, one pair carries everything for the rest, and the stiffness step between them drives gear-mesh vibration.
  • Interference is a tip gouging the flank below the base circle, where no involute exists; avoid it with \( N_{\min}=2k/\sin^2\phi \) — 31.9 at 14.5°, 17.1 at 20°, 11.2 at 25°.
  • That curve is why 20° is standard; 25° buys smaller pinions at 28% more radial bearing load and less contact ratio.
  • Opening the centre distance changes the operating pressure angle, the contact ratio (1.635 to 1.395 for +1 mm) and the backlash (0.73 mm) — but never the speed ratio.
  • Backlash is required for lubricant and thermal growth: it is controlled, not eliminated.

6.lecture:
§1 · Simple and compound trains

A gear pair changes speed by its tooth-count ratio; a train chains pairs together to reach ratios one pair cannot. The arithmetic is bookkeeping.

Key relation — train value

\[ e=\frac{\omega_{\text{out}}}{\omega_{\text{in}}} =\pm\frac{\text{product of driving tooth numbers}}{\text{product of driven tooth numbers}} \]

The sign is negative for each external mesh and positive for each internal (ring) mesh; count the external meshes and the sign follows.

In a simple train every gear sits on its own shaft, so intermediate gears cancel completely — an idler changes the direction of rotation and nothing else. In a compound train two gears share a shaft and turn together, so their ratios multiply. That is the only way to reach a large reduction in a sensible envelope.

Take a two-stage reducer: a 17-tooth pinion driving 51 teeth, then a 19-tooth pinion on the same intermediate shaft driving 76 teeth. Stage ratios are \( 51/17 = 3.00 \) and \( 76/19 = 4.00 \), so the train reduces by 12.00. An input of 1750 rev/min leaves at 145.83 rev/min, and the intermediate shaft runs at \( 1750/3 = 583.33 \) rev/min — a speed that belongs to no nameplate and is exactly the number needed to interpret a vibration spectrum.

Torque goes the other way. Ideally output torque is 12 times input torque; at a realistic 97% per mesh the train delivers \( 12 \times 0.97^2 = 11.29 \) times, and the missing 6% leaves as heat that the casing has to reject.

§2 · Epicyclic trains, where the ordinary rule fails

Let a gear's centre move and the tooth-count bookkeeping collapses, because the ratios were derived for fixed centres. In a planetary (epicyclic) set — sun, planets on a carrier, and a ring — the planets both spin and orbit. The fix is to change observer: ride the carrier, and from there every centre is fixed again.

Key relation — train equation for epicyclics

\[ e=\frac{\omega_L-\omega_A}{\omega_F-\omega_A} \]

\( \omega_A \) is the carrier (arm), \( F \) and \( L \) the first and last gears of the train, and \( e \) is the ordinary train value computed as if the carrier were fixed. Two of the three speeds must be known; the third follows.

Work the standard set: sun 20 teeth, planets 20, ring 60 — the geometric requirement being \( N_r = N_s + 2N_p \), which these satisfy. Taking the sun as first and the ring as last, \( e = -N_s/N_r = -1/3 \): one external mesh sun-to-planet, one internal mesh planet-to-ring, so one sign change, and the planet's own tooth count cancels — a planet in this arrangement is an idler.

Hold the ring, drive the sun at 1500 rev/min, take the output from the carrier:

\[ \frac{0-\omega_A}{1500-\omega_A}=-\frac{1}{3} \;\Longrightarrow\; -3\omega_A = -1500+\omega_A \;\Longrightarrow\; \omega_A = 375\ \text{rev/min} \]

The reduction is 4:1, not 3:1. In closed form, ring held gives \( 1+N_r/N_s \), and the extra 1 is the carrier's own rotation. Reading \( N_r/N_s = 3 \) off the tooth counts is the standard planetary mistake and lands 33% out.

The same set gives other ratios by changing what is held. Hold the carrier instead and it becomes an ordinary reversing train: \( \omega_{\text{ring}} = e\,\omega_{\text{sun}} = -500 \) rev/min. Lock any two members together and the whole set turns as one, at 1:1 — which is how an automatic transmission gets a direct drive out of the same hardware.

The planets themselves are worth a number. From \( (\omega_P-\omega_A)/(\omega_S-\omega_A) = -N_s/N_p = -1 \), the planets spin at \( \omega_P = 375 - (1500-375) = -750 \) rev/min: backwards, and at twice the carrier speed. Planet bearings run at that relative speed while orbiting, which is why they, not the teeth, are often what limits an epicyclic set's life.

§3 · What a train is worth: torque, size and load sharing

Three planets share the load between sun and ring, so each mesh carries roughly a third of the torque — the reason an epicyclic set of a given rating is markedly smaller and lighter than a parallel-shaft one, and the reason it is used where space or weight dominates. The word roughly is doing real work: equal sharing requires accurate spacing and some compliance, and a set with three rigidly located planets is statically indeterminate. Practice floats the sun, or the ring, to let the load equalise.

The input and output are coaxial, which suits an inline drive and removes the offset a parallel-shaft box forces on the layout. Against that, an epicyclic set has more parts, needs tighter geometry, and its ratio range per stage is narrower — roughly 3:1 to 10:1 with the ring held.

§4 · Gear-mesh frequency: the train in a spectrum

Every train writes its own signature into the machine's vibration. Teeth engage at a rate set by the shaft speed and the tooth count, and Lesson 5 supplied the mechanism: contact ratio has a fractional part, so mesh stiffness rises and falls once per tooth.

Key relation — gear-mesh frequency

\[ f_{\text{GMF}}=\frac{N\times \text{rev/min}}{60} \]

Computed on either gear of a mesh — the two give the same number, which is the check that the shaft speed used was the right one.

For the two-stage reducer: the first mesh runs at \( 17 \times 1750/60 = 495.8 \) Hz, and the second at \( 19 \times 583.33/60 = 184.7 \) Hz. Neither equals a shaft speed, and both are predictable before the machine is ever started. An analyst who has computed them can name a peak; one who has not sees an unexplained line at 496 Hz.

Epicyclic sets are computed the same way, in the carrier's frame: \( f = N_r|\omega_A-\omega_{\text{ring}}|/60 = 60(375)/60 = 375 \) Hz, and equally \( N_s|\omega_S-\omega_A|/60 = 20(1125)/60 = 375 \) Hz. Two routes, one answer — the same kind of independent check the instant centre gave in Lesson 2.

One design choice hides in the tooth counts. This train uses 17 and 51, and \( \gcd(17,51)=17 \), so each pinion tooth meets only \( 51/17 = 3 \) gear teeth, the same three for the life of the box. Any damage on that pinion tooth is hammered into those three and nowhere else. Choosing 52 instead of 51 makes the counts coprime — a hunting pair — so every pinion tooth eventually meets every gear tooth and wear distributes. The cost is only that the ratio becomes \( 52/17 = 3.0588 \) and the train 12.235, with the output at 143.03 rev/min instead of 145.83. Ratios that come out exact are a warning sign, not a convenience.

quiz.q:
A two-stage compound reducer

Problem. A 17-tooth pinion drives a 51-tooth gear; on the same intermediate shaft a 19-tooth pinion drives a 76-tooth gear. The input runs at 1750 rev/min and delivers 45 N·m. Find the overall ratio, the output speed, the intermediate shaft speed, and the output torque at 97% efficiency per mesh.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Stage ratios: \( 51/17 = 3.000 \) and \( 76/19 = 4.000 \); overall \( 3.000 \times 4.000 = 12.000 \).

(2) Output speed \( = 1750/12 = 145.83\ \mathrm{rev/min} \).

(3) Intermediate shaft \( = 1750/3 = 583.33\ \mathrm{rev/min} \).

(4) Efficiency \( = 0.97^2 = 0.9409 \), so the torque multiplication is \( 12 \times 0.9409 = 11.29 \) and \( T_{\text{out}} = 45 \times 11.29 = 508\ \mathrm{N\cdot m} \).

Answer: 12:1, 145.83 rev/min out, 583.33 rev/min on the intermediate shaft, and 508 N·m. Sanity check: the ideal output torque would be \( 45\times12 = 540 \) N·m, so 32 N·m — about 6% — is lost. Check it as power: input \( P = T\omega = 45(1750)(2\pi/60) = 8.25 \) kW, output \( 508(145.83)(2\pi/60) = 7.76 \) kW, a difference of 0.49 kW that leaves as heat through the casing. That number is the one the thermal design needs, and it is invisible if only speeds are computed.

quiz.q:
A planetary set, three ways

Problem. A planetary set has a 20-tooth sun, 20-tooth planets and a 60-tooth ring. (a) Confirm the set is geometrically possible. (b) With the ring held and the sun driven at 1500 rev/min, find the carrier speed and the ratio. (c) Find the planet speed. (d) With the carrier held instead and the sun still at 1500, find the ring speed.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (a) \( N_r = N_s + 2N_p \): \( 60 = 20 + 2(20) \) ✓.

(b) With the carrier notionally fixed, sun to ring is one external and one internal mesh, so \( e = -N_s/N_r = -20/60 = -1/3 \). Then \( \frac{\omega_r-\omega_A}{\omega_s-\omega_A} = \frac{0-\omega_A}{1500-\omega_A} = -\frac{1}{3} \), giving \( -3\omega_A = -1500 + \omega_A \), so \( \omega_A = 375\ \mathrm{rev/min} \) and the ratio is \( 1500/375 = 4.00 \).

(c) For sun to planet, \( e = -N_s/N_p = -1 \), so \( \frac{\omega_P-375}{1500-375} = -1 \) and \( \omega_P = 375 - 1125 = -750\ \mathrm{rev/min} \).

(d) With the carrier held, the set becomes an ordinary train: \( \omega_r = e\,\omega_s = -\tfrac{1}{3}(1500) = -500\ \mathrm{rev/min} \).

Answer: (a) valid; (b) 375 rev/min, 4.00:1; (c) −750 rev/min; (d) −500 rev/min. Sanity check: the closed form \( 1+N_r/N_s = 1+3 = 4 \) confirms (b), and the difference from the tooth-count ratio of 3 is the carrier's own rotation — a 33% error if it is forgotten. The planets turning at −750 rev/min, twice the carrier speed and backwards, is the number the planet bearings actually see; it is easy to miss because no shaft outside the gearbox turns at it.

quiz.q:
Naming the lines in a gearbox spectrum

Problem. For the compound reducer above (17/51 then 19/76, input 1750 rev/min), find the gear-mesh frequency of each stage. For the planetary set above, find its mesh frequency by two independent routes. Then say what \( \gcd(17,51) \) implies, and what changing 51 to 52 would cost.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) First stage: \( f = 17(1750)/60 = 495.8\ \mathrm{Hz} \). Checked on the other gear: \( 51(583.33)/60 = 495.8\ \mathrm{Hz} \) ✓.

(2) Second stage: \( f = 19(583.33)/60 = 184.7\ \mathrm{Hz} \); on the 76-tooth gear, \( 76(145.83)/60 = 184.7\ \mathrm{Hz} \) ✓.

(3) Planetary, from the ring: \( f = N_r|\omega_A-\omega_r|/60 = 60(375-0)/60 = 375\ \mathrm{Hz} \). From the sun: \( N_s|\omega_s-\omega_A|/60 = 20(1500-375)/60 = 20(18.75) = 375\ \mathrm{Hz} \) ✓.

(4) \( \gcd(17,51) = 17 \), so each pinion tooth meets only \( 51/17 = 3 \) gear teeth, the same three always. With 52 teeth, \( \gcd(17,52)=1 \) and every pinion tooth eventually meets every gear tooth. The cost is the ratio: \( 52/17 = 3.0588 \), overall 12.235, output 143.03 rev/min instead of 145.83, and the first-stage mesh unchanged at 495.8 Hz while the second becomes 181.2 Hz.

Answer: 495.8 Hz and 184.7 Hz; the planetary at 375 Hz confirmed twice; 17/51 is not a hunting pair, and 17/52 costs a 1.9% ratio change to become one. Sanity check: computing each mesh frequency on both of its gears is a genuine check, because the two calculations use different tooth counts and different shaft speeds and can only agree if the speeds were right. Note that no mesh frequency coincides with any shaft speed here (29.2, 9.7 and 2.4 Hz), so a spectrum from this box has three well-separated families of lines.

quiz.q: In a simple gear train, an idler gear
choices: multiplies the ratio by its tooth count
divides the ratio by its tooth count
cancels from the ratio and only changes the direction of rotation
quiz.solution: The idler is driven by the gear before it and drives the gear after it, so its tooth count appears once in the numerator and once in the denominator and cancels exactly. What it does change is the sign: each external mesh reverses direction, so an idler flips the output's sense and lets a designer bridge a centre distance without altering the ratio.

quiz.q: A planetary set has a 20-tooth sun and a 60-tooth ring. The ring is held and the sun is driven. The reduction to the carrier is
quiz.solution: \( 1 + N_r/N_s = 1 + 3 = 4 \). The extra 1 is the carrier's own rotation: the output member is itself moving while the sun turns, which is exactly what the fixed-centre tooth-count rule cannot represent. Reading 3:1 straight off the tooth counts is the standard planetary error and puts every downstream speed and torque 33% out.

quiz.q: In the train equation \( e=(\omega_L-\omega_A)/(\omega_F-\omega_A) \), \( e \) is
choices: the ordinary train value computed as if the carrier were fixed
quiz.solution: \( e \) is the fixed-centre ratio from first to last gear, sign included, worked out as though an observer were riding the carrier. Subtracting \( \omega_A \) from both speeds is what puts the equation into that observer's frame. The actual input-to-output ratio is what the equation is then solved for, and it generally differs from \( e \).

quiz.q: The geometric condition for a standard planetary set to assemble at all is
quiz.solution: The planet has to span the gap between the sun and the ring, and it sits on both sides of its own centre, so the ring's radius exceeds the sun's by two planet diameters — in tooth counts, \( N_r = N_s + 2N_p \). The worked set, 20 + 2(20) = 60, satisfies it. A second condition, that the planets be equally spaced, requires \( (N_s+N_r) \) to divide by the number of planets.

quiz.q: A two-stage reducer has stage ratios 3.00 and 4.00 and 97% efficiency per mesh. The output torque is
quiz.solution: Speed reduction multiplies torque by the ratio and losses take some back: \( 12 \times 0.97^2 = 12 \times 0.9409 = 11.29 \). Efficiencies multiply through a train exactly as ratios do, one factor per mesh. The 6% that does not arrive as torque leaves as heat, and on an 8.25 kW input that is about 0.49 kW the casing has to reject.

quiz.q: A gearbox with a 17-tooth input pinion runs at 1750 rev/min. A vibration spectrum shows a strong line at 496 Hz. This is
quiz.solution: \( f = N\,n/60 = 17(1750)/60 = 495.8 \) Hz. The shaft itself turns at \( 1750/60 = 29.2 \) Hz, nowhere near it. Mesh frequencies are computable before the machine is started, which is what makes them the first thing to calculate when a spectrum is taken — an unexplained line becomes a named one, and only the genuinely unexplained lines then need chasing.

quiz.q: A gear pair with 17 and 51 teeth is described as "not a hunting pair". The consequence is
choices: each pinion tooth meets only three gear teeth, so damage stays concentrated
the mesh frequency cannot be computed
quiz.solution: \( \gcd(17,51)=17 \), so a given pinion tooth returns to the same \( 51/17 = 3 \) gear teeth for the life of the box. Any damage on it is transferred into those three and nowhere else, and wear never distributes. Coprime counts — 17 and 52 — make every tooth eventually meet every other tooth. The ratio is exact either way; that is the point, since an exactly integer ratio is usually a sign the counts share a factor.

quiz.q:
Compared with a parallel-shaft reducer of the same rating, an epicyclic set is smaller mainly because

",
choices: several planets share the torque between sun and ring
quiz.solution: With three planets each mesh carries roughly a third of the torque, so the same rating fits into much less face width and diameter; the coaxial input and output save further space. The word "roughly" matters — equal sharing needs accurate spacing and some deliberate compliance, which is why the sun or ring is usually left to float. Tooth strength and lubrication requirements are the same as for any other gear.

6.kuwait:
Applied case — the planetary that was specified 33% wrong. A pump skid was re-rated and the drive reducer replaced with a compact planetary unit: 20-tooth sun, 20-tooth planets, 60-tooth ring, ring held, motor on the sun at 1500 rev/min, output from the carrier. The specification sheet recorded the reduction as 3:1 from the tooth counts \( N_r/N_s = 60/20 \), and the pump was selected for 500 rev/min. Commissioned, the pump ran at 375 and never reached its duty point.

The train equation is not optional for a moving-centre train. With the carrier notionally fixed, \( e = -N_s/N_r = -1/3 \); with the ring actually held, \( (0-\omega_A)/(1500-\omega_A) = -1/3 \) gives \( \omega_A = 375 \) rev/min, a reduction of \( 1+N_r/N_s = 4 \), not 3. The extra unit is the carrier's own rotation, and no amount of tooth-count arithmetic will produce it. Every downstream figure inherited the error: flow, head and absorbed power were all quoted against a shaft speed 33% too high.

Two practices follow. An epicyclic ratio is never read off tooth counts — it is solved from \( e=(\omega_L-\omega_A)/(\omega_F-\omega_A) \), and the answer states which member is held, because the same hardware gives 4:1, 3:1 reversing or 1:1 depending on that alone. And a commissioning check should include a measured output shaft speed against the calculated one: it takes a tachometer and one minute, and it is the only test that catches a ratio error before the process does.
6.recap:
• Train value \( e = \pm\prod N_{\text{driving}}/\prod N_{\text{driven}} \), one sign change per external mesh; idlers cancel and only reverse direction.
  • Compound trains multiply stage ratios: 51/17 then 76/19 gives 12:1, so 1750 rev/min in leaves at 145.83, with the intermediate shaft at 583.33.
  • Torque multiplies by the ratio less the losses: \( 12\times0.97^2 = 11.29 \), and the missing 6% is heat the casing must reject.
  • Fixed-centre arithmetic fails for epicyclics because the planet centres move; the fix is to ride the carrier.
  • Train equation \( e=(\omega_L-\omega_A)/(\omega_F-\omega_A) \), with \( e \) evaluated as if the carrier were fixed.
  • Sun 20, planets 20, ring 60 (satisfying \( N_r=N_s+2N_p \)): ring held and sun at 1500 gives a carrier at 375 rev/min — \( 1+N_r/N_s = 4 \), not 3.
  • The same set gives −500 rev/min at the ring with the carrier held, and 1:1 with any two members locked together.
  • Planets spin at −750 rev/min, twice carrier speed and backwards — the speed the planet bearings actually see.
  • Three planets share the torque, which is why an epicyclic set of a given rating is smaller; equal sharing needs a floating sun or ring.
  • Gear-mesh frequency \( f = Nn/60 \): 495.8 Hz and 184.7 Hz for the two stages, 375 Hz for the planetary confirmed by two independent routes.
  • \( \gcd(17,51)=17 \) means each pinion tooth meets only three gear teeth for life; 17/52 is a hunting pair and distributes wear, at a 1.9% change in ratio.

7.lecture:
§1 · From motion to force, in one step

Lessons 2 and 3 delivered the kinematics: every link's velocity and acceleration for a given input. This lesson converts them into the numbers that size hardware — pin loads, bearing loads and the torque the motor must actually supply.

The bridge is d'Alembert's principle. A link with mass \( m \) whose centre of mass accelerates at \( \mathbf{a}_G \), while the link itself has angular acceleration \( \alpha \), can be treated as being in static equilibrium if two fictitious quantities are added to its free-body diagram: an inertia force \( -m\mathbf{a}_G \) at the centre of mass, and an inertia couple \( -I_G\alpha \). With those in place the whole apparatus of statics applies unchanged — sum forces to zero, sum moments to zero — on a machine that is plainly not static.

Key relations — d'Alembert and the offset force

\[ \sum\mathbf{F}-m\mathbf{a}_G=0,\qquad \sum M_G-I_G\alpha=0,\qquad e=\frac{I_G\alpha}{m\,a_G} \]

The force and the couple can be combined into a single equivalent offset inertia force of the same magnitude \( ma_G \), displaced a distance \( e \) from the centre of mass — one vector instead of two quantities.

Take a connecting rod of 0.8 kg with \( I_G = 0.0045\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} \), whose centre of mass accelerates at 1200 m/s² while the rod's angular acceleration is 4000 rad/s². The inertia force is \( 0.8(1200) = 960 \) N and the inertia couple \( 0.0045(4000) = 18 \) N·m, so the equivalent single force is 960 N applied \( 18/960 = 18.75 \) mm off the centre of mass. That offset is not a detail: it is what decides how the 960 N divides between the two pins at the ends of the rod.

§2 · Static analysis: what the motor owes the load

Strip the inertia away first and ask a purely static question. The four-bar of Lessons 1 and 2 — ground 100, crank 40, coupler 120, rocker 90 mm — resists a 50 N·m torque at the rocker. What torque does the crank need?

The coupler is a two-force member: no load acts along its length, so it can only push or pull along its own line. Its force therefore produces a moment about \( O_4 \) of \( F\,r_4\sin\mu \), where \( \mu \) is the transmission angle. At \( \theta_2 = 60^\circ \), \( \mu = 46.38^\circ \), so

\[ F=\frac{T_4}{r_4\sin\mu}=\frac{50}{0.090\sin 46.38^\circ}=767.4\ \mathrm{N} \]

and the same force acting on the crank at A, at \( 60^\circ - 24.95^\circ = 35.05^\circ \) to it, needs a crank torque of \( 767.4(0.040)\sin 35.05^\circ = 17.63\ \mathrm{N\cdot m} \).

Check that against power. Nothing stores or dissipates energy in an ideal linkage, so \( T_2\omega_2 = T_4\omega_4 \) and \( T_2 = 50(3.525)/10 = 17.63\ \mathrm{N\cdot m} \). The two routes agree exactly, and they share no arithmetic — one is a moment balance through the coupler, the other a power balance using Lesson 2's velocity ratio. This is the third time in this course that an independent check has been available; it is worth the thirty seconds every time.

§3 · Why the transmission angle is a hardware cost

Read the coupler-force equation again: \( F = T_4/(r_4\sin\mu) \). The duty \( T_4 \) is fixed by the process, and \( r_4 \) by the geometry, so the force in the coupler is governed entirely by \( \sin\mu \) — and \( \mu \) sweeps through the cycle.

The figure plots it. At \( \theta_2=180^\circ \), \( \mu=82.3^\circ \) and the coupler carries 561 N. At \( \theta_2=0 \), \( \mu=29.0^\circ \) and it carries 1148 N — 2.05 times as much, for exactly the same useful output. Every pin, every bearing and the coupler section itself are sized by that 1148 N. Lesson 1 called a low transmission angle a grading matter; here is the invoice.

It also explains the fatigue duty. The load is not steady at some average: it cycles between 561 and 1148 N once per revolution, so the pins see a fluctuating load with a mean of about 850 N and an amplitude near 300 N, which is a Goodman problem, not a static one.

§4 · Adding the inertia, and reading the bearing load honestly

The full analysis superposes the two. Work link by link, starting from the link whose acceleration is fully known, and carry the pin forces along the chain:

  1. From the kinematics, get \( \mathbf{a}_G \) and \( \alpha \) for every link.
  2. Put the inertia force and couple on each link's free-body diagram.
  3. Solve the links in sequence, transferring the pin force from one to the next.
  4. The crank torque that emerges is the shaking torque; the resultant force on the frame is the shaking force, and it is what the foundation feels.

The scale of the inertia contribution is easy to underrate. A 0.5 kg piston at the 2500 m/s² of Lesson 3 delivers 1250 N through its pin at top dead centre with no gas load at all — larger than the entire static coupler force computed above, from a part that weighs half a kilogram. In fast machinery the inertia terms dominate and the static analysis is the small correction, which is the reverse of the intuition most people bring from statics.

Two practical consequences. First, bearing selection needs the peak load and its direction, both of which move through the cycle; a mean value understates the duty and hides the fact that the load reverses. Second, the shaking force is the reason machinery is bolted down and the reason balancing exists — and balancing is Lesson 10.
7.foundations:
What this lesson assumes

  • Acceleration analysis (Lesson 3) — supplies \( \mathbf{a}_G \) and \( \alpha \) for every link, without which no force can be computed.
  • Transmission angle (Lesson 1) — reappears here as the divisor that sets the coupler force.
  • Two-force members (Statics L3) — why the coupler's force acts along its own line.
  • Moment equilibrium (Statics L2) — applied to a moving machine via d'Alembert.
  • Fluctuating-load fatigue (Machine Design I L4) — the pin load cycles once per revolution, so it is a Goodman problem.

quiz.q:
Crank torque, two independent ways

Problem. The four-bar of Lesson 2 — ground 100, crank 40, coupler 120, rocker 90 mm — is at \( \theta_2=60^\circ \), where \( \theta_3=24.95^\circ \), \( \theta_4=71.34^\circ \), \( \mu=46.38^\circ \) and \( \omega_4/\omega_2=0.3525 \). The rocker resists 50 N·m. Find the coupler force and the required crank torque, then check the torque by a power balance.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The coupler is a two-force member, so its force acts along AB. Its moment about \( O_4 \) is \( F r_4\sin\mu \), which must equal 50 N·m:

\( F = \dfrac{50}{0.090\sin 46.38^\circ} = \dfrac{50}{0.090(0.72396)} = \dfrac{50}{0.065156} = 767.4\ \mathrm{N} \).

(2) The same force acts on the crank at A. The angle between the crank and the coupler is \( 60^\circ - 24.95^\circ = 35.05^\circ \), so

\( T_2 = F r_2\sin 35.05^\circ = 767.4(0.040)(0.57424) = 17.63\ \mathrm{N\cdot m} \).

(3) Power check: an ideal linkage neither stores nor dissipates, so \( T_2\omega_2 = T_4\omega_4 \) and \( T_2 = 50(0.3525) = 17.63\ \mathrm{N\cdot m} \).

Answer: coupler force 767.4 N, crank torque 17.63 N·m, confirmed by power. Sanity check: the two routes agree to four figures while sharing no arithmetic — one is a moment balance through the coupler geometry, the other uses only the velocity ratio from Lesson 2. Note also that the crank torque is far smaller than the rocker torque, by exactly the velocity ratio, which is what a speed increase from crank to rocker must cost in torque.

quiz.q:
What the worst transmission angle costs

Problem. The same linkage holds the same 50 N·m at the rocker through a whole revolution. Using \( \mu_{\min}=28.955^\circ \) at \( \theta_2=0 \) and \( \mu_{\max}=82.284^\circ \) at \( \theta_2=180^\circ \), find the largest and smallest coupler forces, their ratio, and the mean and amplitude of the pin load.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) At \( \mu_{\min} \): \( F = \dfrac{50}{0.090\sin 28.955^\circ} = \dfrac{50}{0.090(0.48423)} = 1147.6\ \mathrm{N} \).

(2) At \( \mu_{\max} \): \( F = \dfrac{50}{0.090\sin 82.284^\circ} = \dfrac{50}{0.090(0.99098)} = 560.6\ \mathrm{N} \).

(3) Ratio \( = 1147.6/560.6 = 2.05 \).

(4) Mean \( = (1147.6+560.6)/2 = 854.1\ \mathrm{N} \); amplitude \( = (1147.6-560.6)/2 = 293.5\ \mathrm{N} \).

Answer: 1147.6 N and 560.6 N, a factor of 2.05; the pins see \( 854 \pm 294 \) N. Sanity check: the output has not changed at any point in the cycle — the machine does exactly the same work — yet the hardware must be sized for twice the force at one position. That is the whole practical content of the transmission angle. And because the load cycles once per revolution, the pins carry a fluctuating load, so the bushes are a fatigue and fretting problem rather than a static bearing-pressure one.

quiz.q:
Inertia force, inertia couple, and the offset (with a US customary check)

Problem. A connecting rod has mass 0.8 kg and \( I_G = 0.0045\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} \). At the instant considered its centre of mass accelerates at 1200 m/s² and the rod's angular acceleration is 4000 rad/s². Find the inertia force, the inertia couple and the offset of the equivalent single force. Then express the force in pounds-force, and compare it with the 1250 N a 0.5 kg piston delivers at 2500 m/s².
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Inertia force \( = m a_G = 0.8(1200) = 960\ \mathrm{N} \), directed opposite to \( \mathbf{a}_G \).

(2) Inertia couple \( = I_G\alpha = 0.0045(4000) = 18.0\ \mathrm{N\cdot m} \), opposing \( \alpha \).

(3) Offset \( e = \dfrac{I_G\alpha}{m a_G} = \dfrac{18.0}{960} = 0.01875\ \mathrm{m} = 18.75\ \mathrm{mm} \).

(4) \( 960\ \mathrm{N} \div 4.448 = 215.8\ \mathrm{lbf} \).

(5) The piston delivers \( 0.5(2500) = 1250\ \mathrm{N} \), 30% more than the rod, from a part of 0.5 kg against the rod's 0.8 kg.

Answer: 960 N (215.8 lbf), 18.0 N·m, offset 18.75 mm; the lighter piston contributes the larger force.

Sanity check: the comparison is the useful part. Mass is a poor guide to inertia loading because acceleration varies so much more than mass does across a mechanism — the piston is 60% of the rod's mass and sees more than twice its acceleration. The offset also deserves a second look: 18.75 mm on a rod a few hundred millimetres long is small, but it is what splits the 960 N unequally between the two pins, and ignoring it puts the wrong number into each bearing.

quiz.q: d'Alembert's principle allows a moving link to be analysed by statics provided that
choices: an inertia force and an inertia couple are added to its free body
quiz.solution: Adding \( -m\mathbf{a}_G \) at the centre of mass and \( -I_G\alpha \) about it converts the dynamic problem into an equilibrium problem that the usual force and moment sums solve. Speed is irrelevant — the faster the machine, the larger those added terms and the more they dominate. Friction is a separate modelling choice, and the link is emphatically not in equilibrium; the principle is a bookkeeping device that lets it be treated as if it were.

quiz.q: The equivalent offset inertia force replaces a force and a couple with a single force displaced by
quiz.solution: Moving a force sideways by \( e \) generates a couple \( F e \), so to reproduce \( I_G\alpha \) with a force \( ma_G \), the offset must be \( e = I_G\alpha/(ma_G) \) — 18.75 mm in the worked rod. The point of the substitution is that a single displaced vector can be carried directly into a graphical or free-body solution, where a separate couple is easy to lose.

quiz.q: A four-bar coupler carries \( F = T_4/(r_4\sin\mu) \). Halving \( \sin\mu \) at constant output torque
quiz.solution: \( \sin\mu \) is in the denominator, so halving it doubles the force in the coupler and in both its pins — while the useful output is unchanged. In the worked linkage that is very nearly what happens between the best and worst positions: 561 N against 1148 N, a factor of 2.05. Output power is set by the load and the speed and is untouched by geometry.

quiz.q: In an ideal frictionless linkage, the crank torque required for an output torque \( T_4 \) is
quiz.solution: Power in equals power out, so \( T_2\omega_2 = T_4\omega_4 \) and \( T_2 = T_4\,\omega_4/\omega_2 \) — \( 50(0.3525) = 17.63 \) N·m for the worked case. Because the ratio varies through the cycle, so does the required crank torque, which is precisely the fluctuating torque a flywheel is fitted to smooth.

quiz.q: A 0.5 kg piston accelerating at 2500 m/s² delivers a pin force of
choices: it depends on the gas pressure only
quiz.solution: \( F = ma = 0.5(2500) = 1250 \) N, from inertia alone and before any gas load is added. It is larger than the entire static coupler force in the worked four-bar, from a part weighing half a kilogram — the standard demonstration that in fast machinery the inertia terms dominate and the static analysis is the correction.

quiz.q: An ideal four-bar drives a constant output torque at a constant input speed. The torque the crank must supply
choices: varies through the cycle, because the velocity ratio varies
is zero at the toggle positions only
quiz.solution: \( T_2 = T_4\,\omega_4/\omega_2 \), and Lesson 2 showed that ratio sweeping from 0.0014 to 0.838 in this linkage. A constant load therefore demands a crank torque that rises and falls once per revolution even with a perfectly steady motor and no friction. That fluctuation, together with the inertia terms, is what a flywheel is fitted to absorb — Lesson 9.

quiz.q: The shaking force of a mechanism is
choices: the resultant force transmitted to the frame and foundation
the inertia couple on the crank
quiz.solution: It is the resultant of all the inertia effects, delivered into the frame through the bearings, and it is what a foundation and its holding-down bolts actually feel. It is the quantity balancing exists to reduce (Lesson 10). The shaking torque is its rotational partner, and is what a flywheel smooths (Lesson 9).

quiz.q: A bearing is selected using the average of the load over the cycle rather than the peak. The consequence is
choices: the peak contact pressure and the load reversal are both missed
no consequence if the average is correct
quiz.solution: Bearing capacity is set by peak contact pressure, and life by the load spectrum, so averaging discards exactly the information that matters — in the worked linkage the peak is 1148 N against a mean of 854 N, 34% higher. Averaging also hides the reversal: a load that swings between two values fatigues and frets a bush in a way a steady load does not.

7.kuwait:
Applied case — the bushes that only wore on one machine. Two identical conveyor drives, same duty and same drive motor, used four-bar linkages built by different fabricators to the same nominal stroke. One ran for years on its original pins. The other consumed coupler bushes at roughly three times the rate, and the maintenance record blamed lubrication.

Measurement of the two linkages found link lengths within a few millimetres of each other but in a different combination, and that was enough. With the output torque fixed by the process, the coupler force is \( F = T_4/(r_4\sin\mu) \), so the peak load through the pins is set by the worst transmission angle in the cycle. Working the geometry of the poor machine gave \( \mu_{\min}=29.0^\circ \) against the good machine's much healthier figure: at 50 N·m of rocker torque, that is a peak coupler force of 1148 N instead of 561 N, once every revolution, for the life of the machine. Nothing was wrong with the lubricant or the bush material; the geometry was asking for twice the load.

Two practices follow. A linkage's bearing duty is a geometry calculation, not a load calculation: the same output torque produces very different pin forces depending on proportions, and the number to compute is the peak over the cycle. And when two nominally identical machines wear at different rates, comparing the link lengths costs nothing and settles whether the difference is in the maintenance or in the drawing.
7.recap:
• d'Alembert converts a moving link into a statics problem: add an inertia force \( -m\mathbf{a}_G \) and an inertia couple \( -I_G\alpha \) to its free body.
  • The two combine into one equivalent offset inertia force, displaced by \( e = I_G\alpha/(ma_G) \) — 18.75 mm for the worked rod, and what splits the load between its two pins.
  • A coupler is a two-force member, so its force acts along its own line and its moment about the rocker pivot is \( Fr_4\sin\mu \).
  • The worked four-bar at \( \theta_2=60^\circ \) needs 767.4 N in the coupler and 17.63 N·m at the crank for 50 N·m at the rocker.
  • The power balance \( T_2\omega_2=T_4\omega_4 \) reproduces 17.63 N·m exactly, sharing no arithmetic with the force route — use it every time.
  • \( F=T_4/(r_4\sin\mu) \) makes the transmission angle a hardware cost: the same duty needs 1148 N at \( \mu=29.0^\circ \) and 561 N at \( 82.3^\circ \), a factor of 2.05.
  • That load cycles once per revolution — \( 854\pm294 \) N — so the pins are a fatigue and fretting problem, not a static bearing-pressure one.
  • Inertia usually dominates: a 0.5 kg piston at 2500 m/s² puts 1250 N through its pin, more than the entire static coupler force.
  • Solve link by link, carrying pin forces along the chain; what emerges at the frame is the shaking force, and at the crank the shaking torque.
  • Bearings are selected on the peak load and its direction, both of which move through the cycle; an average understates the duty and hides the reversal.
